item.title: Wayland desktop for Linux with skeuomorphic design (122 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://github.com/fyzugx/DEsk, See on Hacker News

English | 日本語

v0.1.2 (BETA) -- v0.1, the first public release, with fixes and an installer for Fedora. See RELEASE-NOTES.md.

I've created a Discord server! You can also report bugs and submit ideas for new features here! link : https://discord.gg/xR5f7Xs49

DEsk is Desktop Environment and desk in one word -- a name that came from the Reddit community. It used to be called DeskWM: the commands are now desk, desk-session, desk-settings and so on, and what was set up for DeskWM (its settings, its data, DESKWM_* variables) carries over by itself.

A Wayland desktop for Linux in realistic skeuomorphism -- the kind iOS 6 had, where everything on the screen is drawn to look like the real thing. Here the desktop is a desk.

Windows are sheets of paper on a walnut desk. The dock is a drawer, your apps are filed in binders on a bookshelf behind the desk, notifications arrive in a post box, and the system controls are a panel built into the back of the desk. The room is ray-traced, and one desk lamp lights all of it.

Status: beta. DEsk is used day to day on its author's machines and has been checked carefully (see docs/ARCHITECTURE.md, section 9), but this is its first release: expect rough edges, and expect things to change. Your settings and data will be carried forward.

Install

Download the latest release from the Releases page and unpack it (or clone this repository). Then, in its folder, run the line for your system:

Debian 13

sudo sh scripts/install_debian.sh

Ubuntu 24.04 / 26.04 (and Linux Mint, Pop!_OS)

sudo sh scripts/install_ubuntu.sh

Arch Linux (and EndeavourOS, Manjaro)

sudo sh scripts/install_arch.sh

Fedora 43 / 44 (and Nobara)

sudo sh scripts/install_fedora.sh

Then log out and choose DEsk on the login screen.

  • It shows what it will install and asks first. --yes takes the suggested answers; --no-apps installs DEsk without the recommended programs.
  • The first login draws the room once: a few seconds on a GPU, longer without one. After that it starts at once.
  • To update, get the new release and run the same line again. Your settings are kept.
  • Something went wrong? See Reporting a problem.

More options, building by hand and running DEsk in a window are under Build and Run.

What's on the desk

Nothing here is a symbol for a thing on a desk. As in the realistic skeuomorphism of iOS 6, each is drawn to look like the real thing set down there -- its material, the light on it, its shadow and the wear of use.

  • Windows are paper. Each window sits on a cream sheet with real fibre, thickness and a dog-eared corner. Hold the pointer on the corner and it lifts to show what is printed on the back: Fold (minimize: folded like a letter and left on the desk, under the windows as paper put down is), Unfold / Refold (maximize and restore), and Discard (close: crumpled into a ball and tossed). Dragging an edge pulls more paper out from behind the sheet.
  • The drawer is the dock. Pull the brass handle (or press Super+D). It holds the things you put in it: any app, or a folded window. Out of the box it holds DEsk's standard programs (below) and a screwdriver that opens Shell Settings.
  • The bookshelf holds your apps (Super+A, or the ALL APPS plate). Each category is a ring binder whose sheets fan from a single ring. Take a sheet and it is carried down to the desk, where the app's window opens on it. At the end of the row stands an ALL APPS index book: every program from A to Z, with thumb tabs and a line at the top of the page to type into (input methods via IBus work).
  • The post box is the notification centre (Super+N). Letters show the sender and subject, and a letter taken out lies on the desk.
  • The Control Panel (Super+C) is a valve-era machine built into the back of the desk: real meters, a volume knob, network and Bluetooth levers, a fader for the room's lamp and one for the screen's own backlight (on a laptop, through logind; the brightness keys work too), a key to unlock the power buttons, and the system tray as paper slips under it (more than fit, and the wheel slides the row along).
  • A desk calendar, a desk memo pad and a clock stand on the shelf. The calendar has a notebook of plans and to-dos, and notes are peeled off and stuck onto the day. The memo pad is taken down the same way and written on (IBus works there too); its sheets turn over the wire. The clock shows the seconds small beside the minutes, under two lamps that light only while a camera or a microphone is in use.
  • The front door is out in the real world. The lock screen's door has the hour's light -- the sun worked out from your time zone's city, the porch lamp coming on at dusk -- and, if you let it ask open-meteo.com for that city's weather (only its latitude and longitude are sent), the weather: rain darkening the brick and streaking past the lamp, snow settling on what faces up, fog, lightning. And on certain days of the year the door and the clock have something more for you -- there is no setting for it; what it is, you will see on the day (give Shell Settings your birthday, and that is one of them). Esc stops it.
  • Light. The room (desk, shelf, console, post box) is ray-traced on the GPU (GLES 3), with a CPU tracer as the fallback, and cached per screen size. Everything drawn over it is lit by the same lamp. At login the room starts dark and the lamp comes up as the room is made, while the clock counts how far in glowing red.
  • Sizes are in points. A bigger screen is a bigger desk, not bigger things.
  • More than one screen. The desk is on one screen; every other shows more of the desk's boards, running on from it, for windows to lie on. A new window comes onto the screen the pointer is on, Unfold and full screen fill the screen the window is on, and nothing the desk's own screen does -- the drawer, turning to the bookshelf -- moves what lies on the others or takes it out of reach. A screen taken away puts its windows on one that is left.
  • X11 apps run through Xwayland, and windows that draw their own frames sit on paper too.
  • The screen lock is the front door (Super+L, or logind): you walk up to it at night, close enough to touch, traced in 3D with its own lamps and soft shadows. Your picture and name are on the board hung on it, the password goes in at the brass plate, the key beside it; on Return (or a click on the key) you lean in and turn the key. Let in, it goes round, the door swings open, you walk through into the room and sit down at the desk; told no, it will not turn. Locking is the same run backwards -- out of the room, the door shut, the key turned -- from Super+L or the blue LOCK button on the Control Panel. Checked with PAM, as at login.
  • Seven languages. Everything DEsk prints itself, and the names of programs, are in English, Japanese, Chinese (simplified), Korean, Spanish, French or German: the locale's, or language = en | ja | zh | ko | es | fr | de in ~/.config/desk/shell.conf (or the Shell Settings app), and switch live. The calendar is printed as one sold there is, and Chinese and Korean are set in their own cut of the CJK faces.

Standard programs

DEsk is meant to be installed as a whole desktop, like GNOME or KDE, so it picks a standard program for each job the desk has: a terminal, a web browser, a file manager and a text editor. The drawer's things and Super+Enter open them. For each job, the first of these that is there:

  1. app.terminal, app.browser, app.files, app.editor in shell.conf (a .desktop id),
  2. the default-applications lists in the freedesktop.org order: ~/.config/desk-mimeapps.list (DEsk only), ~/.config/mimeapps.list (what Shell Settings' Default programs, xfce4-mime-settings, writes), and the same two in the system's folders, ending with the desk-mimeapps.list installed with DEsk -- the same answers xdg-open and GIO give,
  3. the standard set, classic GTK programs first: Xfce Terminal, Firefox ESR, Thunar, Mousepad (then MATE Terminal, Caja, Pluma, and so on),
  4. any program filed under the right category.

A tour
The corner of every window: Fold, Unfold, Discard. The drawer: the dock.
A folded window, lying on the desk under the others. The bookcase behind the desk.
ALL APPS, every program from A to Z ... ... and a line to type into.
The Control Panel. The post box: notifications.
The desk calendar and its notes. Shell Settings.

Documentation

  • docs/ARCHITECTURE.md -- how DEsk is built: the programs, the compositor, the ray-traced room, threads, files.
  • docs/MODDING.md -- changing DEsk: words and languages, settings, borrowed programs, sounds, the room, things on the desk.
  • docs/CONFIGURATION.md -- every setting, file and environment variable.
  • RELEASE-NOTES.md -- what is in v0.1.2 and what is known not to work yet.
  • docs/design.md -- the full development log (in Japanese).

As a desktop

DEsk draws the desk; the work done on it is done with free software that already exists. It reaches completeness by borrowing, and keeps a firm line between what it makes and what it borrows:

DEsk makes both: DEsk draws it, something else does the work borrowed
what what is drawn as the room and handled as its things; what only the compositor can do programs, system settings panels, background helpers
examples windows as paper, the drawer, the bookcase, the clock, the Control Panel, the post box, the front door, the calendar and memo pad; keyboard, pointer and their keys (volume and media keys too), the screens and their power, remembering their arrangement, going idle, the lock; Shell Settings volume knob and mute (PipeWire/PulseAudio), brightness (logind), Wi-Fi and Bluetooth levers, the post box (the desk is the notification daemon), the tray's slips (the applets' own items), the clock's MEDIA page (MPRIS), screenshots (grim), the input method (a bridge to IBus) network connections, Bluetooth devices, sound devices, display arrangement, printers, the look of other programs, default programs, disks, polkit agent, keyring, portals -- and the programs themselves

The rule for new cases: make only what is drawn as part of the room or can only be done inside the compositor; otherwise find an existing program that works as it is under a wlroots compositor, and make something only as a last resort. KDE's System Settings and kcmshell (which do not work outside Plasma), Xfce's and MATE's X11-only dialogs, and Xfce's display and appearance dialogs (which need xfsettingsd, and xfsettingsd overwrites GSettings with Xfce's defaults as it starts) are not used.

sudo sh scripts/install_debian.sh     # DEsk and the whole set (install_ubuntu.sh, install_arch.sh, install_fedora.sh)
sh scripts/install-desktop.sh         # only the programs (shows them, then asks for sudo)
sh scripts/install-desktop.sh --extras   # and the office suite, mail...

install-desktop.sh works with apt, dnf, pacman and zypper. On Debian and Ubuntu the same set is also one package: equivs-build packaging/debian/desk-desktop.equivs.

For What comes
terminal, files, text Xfce Terminal, Thunar (with tumbler and thunar-volman), Mousepad
the web Firefox (Firefox ESR on Debian, the snap on Ubuntu)
pictures, documents, music and video Ristretto, Atril, Parole
tools Engrampa, GNOME Disks
networks, Bluetooth, sound NetworkManager with its applet and editor, Blueman, PipeWire, pavucontrol
displays, looks, defaults wdisplays, nwg-look (GNOME Tweaks on Ubuntu 24.04 and Fedora), Xfce's MIME settings
printing system-config-printer, CUPS
notices udiskie (memory sticks mounted, with a letter), poweralertd (low battery; batsignal on Arch; none on Fedora), package-update-indicator (updates; Debian and Ubuntu)
looking after the machine QDirStat (disk usage), LXQt's date and time and users, Mugshot (your name and picture), Seahorse (passwords and keys), gnome-packagekit (adding and removing programs), Back In Time (backups), Xfce Task Manager, hardinfo2 (about this computer); baobab and Deja Dup on Arch; no Mugshot on Fedora
passwords MATE's polkit agent, GNOME Keyring
plumbing xdg-desktop-portal (wlr, gtk), Xwayland, xdg-user-dirs, xdg-utils, wl-clipboard, grim, curl
looks Qt's GTK platform theme, so Qt programs match the GTK ones
typing and fonts IBus (and Mozc for Japanese), Noto (CJK, emoji), the URW base 35, Klee One (not on Arch or Fedora)
--extras LibreOffice (drawn with GTK), Thunderbird, Galculator, Xfce Task Manager, Simple Scan

The classic GTK programs of Xfce and MATE come first because they are the kind of window the desk's paper is cut for -- a menu bar, plain tools and the document -- and they are light, start quickly and run on Wayland as they are. GTK 3 asks the compositor for its frame through KDE's server-decoration protocol, so they lie on DEsk's paper with its printed heading and no GTK title bar. Windows with a header bar (GNOME's programs, Firefox) keep their own frame, inside a paper margin.

Shell Settings (desk-settings) holds DEsk's own settings -- windows, the size of things, how much is drawn, language, clock, your birthday and the weather, when the screen goes off and whether the desk locks then -- on its Shell tab, and on its System tab rows that open the borrowed programs (network, Bluetooth, sound, displays, printers, the look of other programs, default programs, disks, disk usage, colour profiles, the input method, date and time, your name and picture, users, passwords and keys, adding and removing programs, backups, what the computer is doing, and the Experience Index), classic-looking programs first, each with the program's own icon and its name -- "Displays (wdisplays)" -- so you can see what does the setting. A row whose program is not installed is printed faint with the package to install, by this distribution's name. The two tabs sit on the sheet like a folder's index tabs, and in each pocket is a wire-bound pad with a sheet to each part of the form and a sticky note on each sheet's edge; taking hold of a note turns the sheets over the wire to it, as on the desk calendar (Page Up and Down too). Changing tab (a click, Ctrl+Tab or Ctrl+Page Up/Down) draws the other pad up out of the folder from below, and the pad comes up the same way when the window opens.

Started as a session (desk-session, from a login screen), DEsk tells D-Bus and systemd where its display is, runs the XDG autostart entries (leaving out the ones that would fight it, such as another notification daemon or an X screen locker), and starts an authentication agent, the keyring, the input method and the network applet with whichever free program for each is installed. The input method's candidates come up under the text being written -- in a program's window as on the desk's own pages -- and leave the keys where they are. It turns the screen off when nobody is at the desk (locking first, by default), lets video players keep it on, and speaks wlr-output-management (wdisplays, wlr-randr, kanshi), remembering a display tool's arrangement for each set of screens. Logging out, restarting and powering off ask every window to close first, so a program with unsaved work can ask about it; a window that does not close holds it up and is put in front.

Shell Settings also sets what only a Wayland compositor can: tap to click, natural scrolling, pointer speed and left-handed buttons (through libinput), the keyboard layout, a second layout and the keys that change to it, and key repeat -- applied at once to what is plugged in.

How much the desk draws is a setting too, Graphics: Ultra (the room traced finer, and wider where a GPU can, and nothing drawn coarser while it moves), High (as made, the default), Medium, Low, and 2D Fallback -- for a machine without a GPU or a virtual machine rendering on its CPU: no shadows, nothing fading, blurred or moving, nothing ray-traced as it moves, and the room traced once, small and plain. On two CPU cores without a GPU the first start goes from nearly ten minutes to about a quarter of a minute, and a frame from 2 ms to 0.5 ms. The installer takes a quick look at the machine (desk-index --suggest: the graphics, or the processor, for a couple of seconds, the threads and the memory, and how long the processor takes to draw a sheet of paper folding) and picks the level for it, as the machine's default (/etc/xdg/desk/shell.conf); each user's own choice wins.

Where the screen is drawn by the processor -- no GPU, a virtual machine without 3D, a GPU without its driver -- the desk runs in 2D Fallback unless you choose a level yourself, and says so: a letter in the post box (check the graphics drivers, or the virtual machine's settings) and a line in red beside Graphics in Shell Settings. 2D Fallback is the same desk with its effects off, not a second one, its room traced at a sample a pixel and softened. And a first start, which traces the room from nothing, leaves a letter in the middle of the desk saying it may take a minute or two, more on some machines, and that the desk can be used meanwhile.

It is meant to stay light on old machines. Measured on a machine held to about a 2010 laptop's pace (a quarter of a core each on two cores, 2 GB, no GPU for the room): a later login shows the desk in under half a second and has the light on in 1.4 s; the very first one, which has to trace the room on the processor, shows a soft first look and the light within seven seconds instead of a minute and a half in the dark; folding a sheet costs 5 ms a frame at Low. The traced room is kept across updates, and paper in motion is drawn finer or coarser by the level (whole at High, half at Low).

Programs on the desk are dressed for it too: DEsk's own icons, drawn to look like the real things set down on the desk, the way iOS 6 drew them -- manila card folders with papers in them, a typed page with its corner turned down, a letter signed in blue ink, a ledger, slides in their mounts, instant photos, a record sliding out of its sleeve, a film slate, a taped carton for an archive, a deck of punched cards for a program, a block of wood type for a font, a wire wastebasket you see through, a brass globe for the network, a drive in its aluminium case -- with the grain of paper, card, wood and brushed metal and the shadows they cast; and a GTK theme of paper, ink and brass. They are set in a dconf layer of DEsk's own over the user's, so another desktop on the same machine keeps its look.

When something on the desk gets stuck: Ctrl+Alt+Del twice puts everything of the desk's own away and draws it all again (the windows stay as they are); three times logs out. desk-ctl reset and desk-ctl logout do the same from a terminal or another VT.

The DEsk Experience Index

desk-index rates the machine at what the desk asks of it, the way the Windows Experience Index did: processor, memory, 2D graphics (the desk's own drawing), 3D graphics (the room's shader, checked against the CPU) and disk, each 1.0-9.9, on brass-rimmed meters; the base score is the lowest. desk-index --text prints the same in a terminal.

Requirements

The simplest way is the installer for your distribution (below), which brings everything. To build it yourself:

  • wlroots 0.18 (Debian 13 has it, and Fedora 43 and later as wlroots0.18; Ubuntu 24.04 has 0.17, Ubuntu 26.04 only 0.19 and Arch only 0.20, so the installers build 0.18.3 from its release into /opt/desk-wlroots, used by DEsk alone through its run path)
  • wayland, wayland-protocols, xkbcommon, cairo, pixman, fontconfig, libdrm, PAM
  • libsystemd (optional): the notification daemon and the system tray. Build with -Dpost=disabled to leave them out.
  • libpulse (optional): the desk's sounds (-Dsound=disabled)
  • libinput (optional): touchpad and mouse settings
  • EGL, GLES, gbm (optional): ray-trace the room on the GPU. Without them the CPU does it.
  • Xwayland and xcb (optional): X11-only apps.
  • Fonts: the URW base 35 (fonts-urw-base35) and Noto CJK (fonts-noto-cjk); fonts-klee for the memo pad.
  • At run time: grim for screenshots, curl for the weather at the door.

Minimum and recommended

Measured with the CPU, GPU and memory cut down (systemd-run CPUQuota and MemoryMax, taskset; nested, 1440x900, the same hand moves every run). Once the room is traced, even one core without a GPU dropped no frames; a frame costs about 2 ms. Only the first login traces the room: 6-9 s on a GPU, about 10 minutes on two cores without one (then it is cached).

minimum recommended
CPU 2 x86-64 cores (1 works) 4 cores or more
memory 4 GB (DEsk itself 200-450 MB) 8 GB or more
GPU none needed (a long first login) OpenGL ES 3.0 with GBM (Mesa Intel, AMD, Nouveau; VMware's SVGA3D)
screen 1366x768 1440x900 or more
disk about 1 GB (--bare; --no-apps adds what Shell Settings opens) 2-2.7 GB with the whole set
system Debian 13, Ubuntu 24.04 / 26.04 LTS, Arch Linux, Fedora 43 / 44 the same

Build

meson setup build
meson compile -C build

Run

Inside your current session, as a window:

As a session of its own, picked from the login screen (GDM, SDDM, LightDM), use the installer for your system (Install). All four take the same options:

sudo sh scripts/install_debian.sh              # or install_ubuntu.sh, install_arch.sh, install_fedora.sh
sudo sh scripts/install_debian.sh --no-apps    # DEsk, what it needs and what Shell Settings opens
sudo sh scripts/install_debian.sh --bare       # DEsk and what it needs, no programs (containers)
sudo sh scripts/install_debian.sh --prefix /opt/desk

sh scripts/install_session.sh picks the right one by itself and keeps what it says in ~/.local/state/desk/install.log. Each installer does the same (derivatives such as Mint, Pop!_OS, EndeavourOS, Manjaro and Nobara are recognised): packages, a release build in build-install, the PAM file, the login entry, and the removal of what the old name, DeskWM, left behind (after asking). Every program Shell Settings' System tab opens is installed, --no-apps or not, and at the end desk-settings --check lists what each row opens (or which package would bring it). On other distributions, install the requirements and run scripts/install.sh. Or from a TTY: desk-session.

To update, get the new copy and run the installer again the same way ("this updates it", it says): what is installed is replaced, the last build is reused (or made afresh when it cannot be), and your settings and the traced room stay. All the installer says is also kept in ~/.local/state/desk/install.log (the last run's) -- the thing to look at, or send, if it stops part way. A copy made for passing round carries SHA256SUMS, and the installer checks every file against it before building: a copy damaged on its way says which files are wrong and stops (copy it again; if a fresh copy is damaged too, suspect the machine's memory or disk -- memtest86+). A Japanese locale gets the Mozc converter among the suggested programs; IBus itself is installed for everyone but only runs for languages typed through an input method, or when one is set up.

The first start at a new screen size spends a little while ray-tracing the room, on the GPU the screen is drawn with: the desk first, then the bookcase, the Control Panel and the post box, each there to turn to as soon as its picture is, and last the films of the camera moves to them (until a film is done, the move to its view is a cut). Each part is cached as it is done, so a first start cut short picks up where it stopped. What DEsk says as it runs is kept in ~/.local/state/desk/session.log (the session before in session.log.old); its desk: room: lines say what the room was traced on and how long each part took -- the thing to send if a start is slow. A GPU is tried once, in a child process, before the room is traced on it; one that fails says why (failed its trial: ...), and the processor traces the room instead -- at High's quality even where Ultra is chosen, Ultra's being a GPU's to trace.

Keys

Key
Super+Enter terminal
Super+Q / Alt+F4 close the focused window
Super+M fold / unfold the focused sheet
Super+D open / close the drawer
Super+A look up at the bookshelf
Super+C the Control Panel
Super+N the post box
Super+Tab / Alt+F1 cycle windows
Esc back to the desk
brightness keys the screen's backlight (or, with none, the lamp)
volume, mute and media keys the mixer and the player playing (as the clock's MEDIA page)
Print / Alt+Print screenshot of the screen / of the window in front
Super+L lock the screen: the front door; type the password, Enter (or click the key)
Super+Esc / Alt+Esc log out (asking the windows to close first)

Reporting a problem

The quickest way: run this in a terminal (any desktop, or a console -- DEsk need not start), and attach the file it writes, ~/desk-report.txt:

It gathers DEsk's version, your Linux, your graphics card and driver, the last session's log and whether DEsk crashed, with your user name, home folder, machine name and network addresses taken out. Read it through before sending it. Say too what you did and what happened.

Without it (an older DEsk, or one not installed), attach by hand:

  • ~/.local/state/desk/session.log (and session.log.old if the problem was in the session before) -- what DEsk said as it ran;
  • if the installer stopped, its last lines from the terminal (or ~/.local/state/desk/install.log when it was run through install_session.sh).

Both are plain text; look them over before sending them. If the desk is stuck, desk-ctl reset from a terminal (or another VT) draws everything again without closing your windows.

How it was made

DEsk was built with the help of AI. Much of the code and the documentation was written by Claude (Anthropic's AI model) under the author's direction: the author decided what DEsk should be and how it should look, tested it on real machines, and reviewed what went in. Reports and patches are welcome all the same.

item.title: Israeli firm's digital ads enabling installation of 'zero-click' spyware (343 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/oct/15/israeli-firm-digital-ads-enabling-installation-of-zero-click-spyware-researchers-say, See on Hacker News

An Israeli advertising agency has been serving millions of online adverts that allow “zero-click” spyware to be used against targets, researchers at a Canadian university have said.

Citizen Lab, a digital investigations research unit at the University of Toronto, said it believed dozens of devices at the Qatari broadcaster Al Jazeera had been compromised by spyware delivered through ads run by Discover-Tech, which describes itself as a specialised digital advertising agency.

According to Citizen Lab, Discover-Tech operates a software platform called Controlium that allows its clients to “mass-profile and deanonymise” internet users then covertly hack targets with third-party spyware. Unlike infections that rely on people interacting with links or files, the spyware requires no interaction from the victim to be installed, making it a new delivery technique, Citizen Lab says.

The infections happen without a user’s knowledge, and in a matter of seconds, according to Citizen Lab.

“[The online advertising] ecosystem is being weaponised at a massive scale to profile millions of users, then silently infect targets with zero-click mercenary spyware,” the report says.

According to the report, Controlium is able to harvest a user’s identity and IP address when the user is shown a seemingly benign custom-created ad – for example, for a digital game or a telecoms service. If the user has been selected as a target for hacking, a mercenary spyware firm can then send a malicious code containing spyware to their device, the researchers say.

They say that millions of users worldwide have been served ads by Discover-Tech since 2024, including in Yemen, Brazil, Mexico and Czechia.

Related work by the research group Confiant also suggests that Discover-Tech’s ads have been shown to users of the networks of government entities in Europe and the US, as well as the UN, Nato, the international criminal court and the International Atomic Energy Agency.

“It’s disastrous that major ad vendors and organisations apparently were neither able to detect nor prevent the company’s malicious advertising operations for years,” said Wolfie Christl, a researcher at Citizen Lab. “The way the online advertising ecosystem works today is a security threat for states, the private sector, civil society and everyone else alike.”

According to Citizen Lab, Controlium acts as a “facilitator” for third-party spyware firms that have targeted “government officials, journalists, businesspeople, activists, academics and embassy workers”. Citizen Lab claims it can deliver spyware that can access everything on the device of a target, extracting messages, photos and emails, recording calls and secretly activating microphones.

The full extent of the targeting allegedly enabled by Discover-Tech is unknown. Citizen Lab’s findings join mounting evidence that the opaque arrangements underpinning the world of online advertising can be leveraged for surveillance.

“There has been a lot of buzz that online ads can be used to identify and automatically hack targets with pinpoint precision, but now for the first time, we have concrete technical evidence showing this process in action,” said Bill Marczak, a researcher at Citizen Lab.

Discover-Tech has been approached for comment.

When a user navigates to a website that shows advertisements, their details become part of a split-second programmatic auction involving dozens or hundreds of companies. These companies bid automatically to place an ad in front of that user.

These bids are based on the user’s profile, which can include information about their device and data compiled on them by tracking their activity across the web. For example, companies given the profile of a 35-year-old interested in sports betting and crypto might bid to show that individual an advertisement for an energy drink.

There is little regulation on this automated online market, and there is growing evidence that it is being exploited by malevolent actors.

Reuters has reported that billions of dollars’ worth of Meta’s ad revenue comes from ads for scams, illegal gambling, pornography and other banned content. In the US, ICE and other government agencies have bought software that uses ad tech data to track people’s movements.

“Cybersecurity agencies, regulators and lawmakers in the US, Europe and other regions must urgently step in. They must investigate the involved companies and fix the systemic risks that enable malicious ad targeting,” said Christl.

Article published by: Leah Rowe

Date of publication: 15 October 2026

  • < Prev

You can find today’s release in https://rsync.libreboot.org/stable/26.10/ or you can use one of the mirrors.

Libreboot is free, open source boot firmware replacing proprietary BIOS/UEFI firmware on supported Intel/AMD and ARM64 hardware. It initialises the hardware inside your computer such as the CPU or memory controller, configuring the machine in such a way as to enable use of an operating system like Linux or BSD at boot - and now Microsoft Windows is also compatible because Libreboot has added full UEFI support via MrChromebox EDK2 payload. Libreboot offers greater security and customisation compared to proprietary firmware; its goal, plainly, is to rid the world of proprietary software and to do that, we therefore try to provide firmware that is extremely easy for non-technical users to understand.

Today’s release changelog is relative to the previous Libreboot 26.01 release.

This is a very special release, with several major design changes made regardless of hardware changes, so users should read this changelog very carefully - and read it twice.

The first major change is:

233 Intel/AMD Chromebooks added

The full list of boards is quite long, so it’s shown at the end of this article. All 233 of them!

MrChromebox supports nearly every Chromebook, and this release imports all boards from that project. This includes everything up to the most recent Intel and AMD hardware.

Imported all 233 currently supported Chromebooks from the MrChromebox coreboot distro. Baytrail (Kip) tested - others need testing. Source-only in this release (must build from source, no binaries provided).

This was done with a utility I wrote at util/mrimport/ which generates configs for lbmk, including revisions and submodules. I made further tweaks manually; further updates upstream can be synced in Libreboot by diffing again the output of mrimport between revisions, adapted into Libreboot irrespective of the latter’s modifications which are numerous - and will be covered next.

Libreboot makes these modifications to MrChromebox coreboot, in its version:

  • Uses the EDK2 UEFI payload for coreboot, provided by MrChromebox; we set the background colour to Libreboot purple, and use the Libreboot rainbow logo instead of the coreboot logo. Our EDK2 build is otherwise currently identical except for the next changes:
  • Set HAP bit by default, at build time, to disable Intel ME. It is not reliably disabled in MrChromebox coreboot by default as most people using it do so via software-based flashing scripts alongside disablement of Google’s security as shown in MrChromebox documentation. We disable it here. NOTE: We also support numerous AMD Chromebooks, which are unrelated in this context.
  • Unlock IFD regions via ifdtool (with quirks properly handled), setting them read-write at build time. This is done instead of modifying every Intel Flash Descriptor provided by MrChromebox, of which there are hundreds.
  • CSMWrap added inside EDK2 (SeaBIOS CSM wrapped in EFI) for backward compatibility with bare metal SeaBIOS as in older Libreboot releases.
  • GRUB EFI build provided inside EDK2, for backward compatibility also - it behaves, from a user’s perspective, exactly like the coreboot-payload version of GRUB and even reads configs from CBFS in the same way.
  • MemTest86+ added inside EDK2.
  • Haswell chromebooks: native raminit used instead of MRC as in upstream.
  • All Intel chromebooks up to Kabylake: use libgfxinit instead of GOP; upstream has since done this on newer gens as well, and this will be integrated post-release.

The additional payloads are, as above, available in the boot menu via ESC keypress at startup. iPXE is also enabled by default, as in upstream, on specific boards. EFI GRUB and CSM SeaBIOS have replaced the coreboot payload versions of these; bare metal SeaBIOS/GRUB are now deprecated and may be removed in a future Libreboot release, although they can be re-enabled by those willing to build Libreboot from source.

This is NOT a fork of MrChromebox, which is to be regarded as Libreboot’s upstream on Intel/AMD Chromebooks. Efforts will be made, as with regular coreboot, to remain as closely in sync with it as possible at all times. I have worked extensively with MrChromebox, and even submitted a few minor fixes to his project; he also implemented CBFS-based VBT and GOP handling per my request, which I will integrate post-release.

Regardless, MrChromebox’s own installation scripts should work, with Libreboot images, so check out MrChromebox documentation for installation. Despite changes, Libreboot’s setup remains behaviourally compatible with the MrChromebox one and, thus, MrChromebox tooling should still work alongside corresponding documentation.

This is made possible by a new feature in Libreboot’s build system: support for an arbitrary number of upstreams per project. We still provide regular coreboot on non-Chromebook mainboards.

Yes, 233. I counted. All automated. My scripting and my fastidiousness ensured that what I imported and configured in lbmk closely matched upstream, and I’m quite careful at maintaining my own divergence from it inside Libreboot.

Yes, Libreboot runs on Chromebooks now!

15h.org fork for Fam15h

E.g. KGPE-D16. We use the coreboot fork from 15h.org now, on AMD Fam15h mainboards. This uses AMD AGESA source code instead of Timothy’s custom init code. It has much more reliable raminit and CPU initialisation; more RAM also supported. Many bugs are fixed. IOMMU works, I also saw that they mentioned TPM is fixed in their version, now our version also.

Regular binaries with SeaBIOS and GRUB payloads provided - we also have experimental EDK2-based images, currently source-only (no binaries available). EDK2 requires a framebuffer to be set up, and the integrated AST2050 chip only starts in text mode on native initialisation; the vendor VGA ROM can set up VESA, but we will not use the VGA ROM. The EDK2-based images are source-only on these boards, intended for use with graphics cards.

Basically, these boards actually work for the first time.

EDK2 UEFI payload by default

EDK2 is Intel’s reference implementation of the UEFI specification, for booting. It’s typically used by vendors, in proprietary forks of Intel’s BSD-licensed code, but Intel’s reference code is Free Software. We use their reference code, and full source code is provided in this Libreboot release. EDK is short for: EFI Development Kit.

More specifically:

We use a fork of EDK2 provided by MrChromebox, which specifically offers use of EDK2 as a generic coreboot payload. This is a complete, industry-standard UEFI implementation capable of booting any compliant operating system.

All. Nearly all boards use it in Libreboot now, even older ones e.g. ThinkPad X200. Tested on all platforms. Older, 32-bit-only mainboards still use the setup from the previous release, while virtually all 64-bit-compatible hardware now use EDK2. EFI builds of GRUB and SeaBIOS are provided in flash, accessible from the EDK2 setup menu (press ESC at boot time when prompted), for backward compatibility with existing Linux/BSD installations in Libreboot.

EDK2 support was integrated as a prerequisite for Chromebooks, but then it was extended for use on all previously existing supported mainboards in Libreboot. It even runs well on really old machines e.g. ThinkPad T500.

All Libreboot boards now use an open source UEFI implementation by default, where feasible. All of them, and it’s by default - the bare metal GRUB and SeaBIOS coreboot payloads have been removed, replaced by EFI versions that are backward compatible.

We previously did not provide UEFI at all, except for U-Boot on a few select mainboards. We now provide full UEFI, with all four freedoms intact, on nearly every mainboard that Libreboot supports.

All of the following operating systems were tested and confirmed working, on various Libreboot machines using EDK2:

  • Windows 10 and 11
  • 9front (fork of Plan 9)
  • various other UEFI-compliant operating systems
  • Linux UKI bootloaders, systemd-boot, etc. UKIs work perfectly now, booting from EDK2. Modern Linux distro setups now work (GRUB not required).
  • OpenBSD with EFI bootloader and GPT partitioning (older SeaBIOS txtmode can only do MBR partitioning in Libreboot)
  • FreeBSD in UEFI mode - txtmode no longer required!
  • ReactOS did not work, unfortunately (no UEFI support)
  • RedoxOS probably works too.

Modern computers and operating systems are all UEFI, and this new setup can boot basically all of it reliably. More testing will be required, but this is battle-tested code and it has been used extensively in coreboot by many users, for many years. Libreboot finally has it as well.

This change alone is part of a much wider effort to modernise Libreboot, and I’m only getting started. The next Libreboot releases will draw heavily on this, as EDK2 is pretty much the expected payload on a lot of modern coreboot setups these days. Integration of EDK2 removes all limitations in Libreboot, allowing us to support much newer hardware and it basically makes Libreboot much easier to use; I expect Libreboot to become much more popular and useful over time, as a result.

Some caveats and extra notes are provided at the end of this release page, for migration purposes. For example, despite boasting about all, older 32-bit-only hardware still use bare GRUB/SeaBIOS. Nearly all boards use EDK2 however!

Modern GPU support (via EDK2)

Finally, some notes about graphics cards that may be of interest to the more demanding users.

EDK2 alongside PCI-E relocatable BAR (rebar) means that you can now use modern graphics cards that require allocations above 4GB. Rebar is not enabled by default, but you can enable it in menuconfig (coreboot). Enabling it causes breakage of Intel GPU video output on libgfxinit in testing, and no fix was found yet, so rebar is disabled by default.

PCI-E Option ROMs are enabled by default where necessary, for EDK2 builds. This means you can use it on desktops with graphics cards. Tested on several desktops (Dell OptiPlex 9020 SFF and 5050 SFF).

On boards with only external GPU, rebar can be left enabled by default. On systems with functioning integrated graphics, accidental enablement of rebar can be remedied by inserting a graphics card; when the video output in the payload does become broken, the Linux i915 video driver still initialises video framebuffer properly in KMS/DRM.

This will be added to general documentation, pending fixes upstream. Note that even with this issue, Linux video output works fine. This will be corrected and rebar enabled by default, on a future Libreboot release.

Feature changes

This is very much a features release. A lot of feature changes were made!

  • EDK2 payload support on all Intel/AMD boards with at least 4MB flash. This uses the MrChromebox version of EDK2, and Libreboot has made extensive modifications e.g. add GRUB EFI and SeaBIOS CSM (CSMwrap) builds to it; these are provided as backward compatibility with older lone SeaBIOS/GRUB payload setups and should still boot existing Linux/BSD installations.
  • iPXE boot method added via EDK2 payload (ESC menu) - only EDK2 (not available in the lone SeaBIOS payload on older boards).
  • Added new command ./mk import_uboot for auto-importing U-Boot configs that can then build in lbmk. Not yet used, but this will be used to add tested U-Boot boards in future releases (U-Boot itself providing its own initialisation). Libreboot can already build U-Boot images from any config, without code changes, only config changes, but testing is needed on hardware.
  • New util at util/mrimport that is used to automatically import/update new configs from MrChromebox coreboot. This was also used for the initial import of 233 chromebooks from MrChromebox, importing them into the Libreboot build system with our own modifications.
  • Added fwsetup command in a GRUB menuentry on the EFI version, which boots back into the edk2 setup menu.
  • Modified IFD on Kabylake boards, for supporting pin mod. This enables use of six- and eight-core Intel CPUs.
  • Randomised MAC addresses at build time, only when XBMK_RELEASE is unset. You can export a MAC address via environmental variable XBMK_MAC to set it arbitrarily. This avoids the need to extract NVM post-build and re-insert, when working directly on .rom files instead of release tarballs, which already have this capability via ./mk inject.
  • GRUB at_keyboard driver: always force scancode set 2 with translation. This was already done, but only on the coreboot target; it is now also done on the EFI target, by just applying it universally to all targets. This is because it’s possible to use it with PS/2 keyboards on EDK2. It mitigates buggy PS/2 controllers that might not report modes correctly even when set, as on the Dell Latitude E6400.
  • I made Memtest86+ purple (on the EDK2 build). Libreboot purple. Red value 0x28, green value 0x0b and blue value 0x22. This is Libreboot Purple.
  • I made EDK2 purple too, and added Libreboot’s rainbow logo to it.
  • Scan every ESP directory in a given partition, via asterisks, on the GRUB payload (EDK2 and coreboot targets). This means that it will boot a larger number of non-UKI Linux distro setups if they use GRUB or Syslinux configs.
  • TPM enabled where available, on all targets that use EDK2.
  • Added ./mk cbtest command which tests board names versus lbmk and coreboot defconfig, in case it changes upstream. Otherwise, we can invisibly change the actual board that builds for a given target if the default one is then chosen by Kconfig rules. There is no way to detect this automatically at build time in a way that is clean, so this command should be used when updating coreboot revisions.
  • Added ./mk test command which aggressively builds everything, much more than even ./mk release - it intentionally disables use of caching, so that downloads are aggressively tested as well. Config-related commands are also tested. This is a brutal stress test command used to find build errors.
  • Flashprog: always keep the flash IC hot during command loops, rather that doing it in a toggle. The --workaround-mx option is retained, but no longer does anything as its behaviour is always applied. This improves general reliability as a lot of users don’t know about this option anyway. More people can reliably flash their boards now.
  • New mkhelper type added: preconfig. This lets you run custom logic prior to configuration on a given project that uses config files. It also works on noconfig projects. This is used for example on coreboot, to build utils.
  • Removed used of ccache everywhere in the build system, as it was causing subtle build errors (and possibly code bugs) in several stress test scenarios. We’d rather wait a bit longer for a reliable build. CCache is really only meant for development, not production.
  • Removed the -c and x (clean and xgcc-clean) flags in lbmk, as they are largely superfluous; lbmk already auto-cleans everything before build anyway, to remove all build artifacts, and aggressively caches builds out of tree based on config metadata, deleting and re-fetching sources from local cache as required. These options were useless.
  • Properly skip builds if makefile checks fail; this allows single-tree projects to build, by preventing error-prone use of copy_elf where no files exist.
  • mk: Removed GCC/GNAT version pairing as upstream (coreboot) now does this its its buildgcc script. It’s redundant in lbmk. The coreboot version is better because it simply errs and exits, instead of trying to continue; the latter is what we did, which might actually cause more bugs in some cases. Better to fail hard, than corrupt the build.
  • Danish keymap added for GRUB.

Design changes

A lot of major design changes have been made!

  • GRUB boot config simplified; only one menuentry now for boot, which boots everything, trying USB first. It selects the first config it finds, but you can press ESC to cycle through to the next one in the loop. Useful for dual-booting multiple Linux distros.
  • Short defconfigs now used on coreboot, instead of full configs. This allows for easier maintenance, and lbmk has been modified to accomodate them. The inject scripts still resolve full configs automatically at runtime, needed for scanning paths at build time. The use of defconfigs reduces the chance of erroneous changes in config during updates, and makes use of olddefconfig possible instead of the less-reliable oldconfig command.
  • New safety check: verify that a path prefix is set, when using it in logic. Otherwise, it’s possible that we might have directory escape bugs in lbmk. This is checked relentlessly, throughout the build system.
  • No longer export XBMK_CACHE as it’s now hardcoded in config. The new handling is much stricter, and less likely to regress in future revision. This was done to reduce the possibility of a directory escape bug in lbmk.
  • Fixed GRUB module list no longer used per GRUB tree. Instead, all modules are added per target but a blacklist is applied, configured per-tree.
  • GRUB Syslinux and GRUB scanning now combined into one function, on GRUB configs. General simplifications to the GRUB config.
  • GRUB is now one source tree, with multiple targets all re-using the very same tree where differing configurations are used.
  • Modified MrChromebox coreboot to only add EDK2 GOP binaries if no video mode is selected in coreboot defconfig. This avoids adding it unnecessarily and thus saving space in the flash, where FSP init or libgfxinit is used.
  • Always use --mirror git clones on include/env/get.sh. This makes cloning revisions more reliable on all projects, especially ones where we use revs inside branches other than main.
  • Auto-unlock IFD regions at build time on all Intel IFD-based systems; disable ME automatically, by setting the HAP bit. This is how we do it on chromebooks, but it’s done on all boards; this mitigates the possibility that we might accidentally forget to neuter the ME on specific targets in the future.
  • When building EDK2, we use coreboot’s build system, but when doing it this way, custom_ prefix is not used in image file names. Proper edk2 prefix is used. This makes it work for Chromebooks, which build edk2 per-board in this release; generalised EDK2 builds aren’t handled on Chromebooks. On non Chromebooks, we build a dummy ThinkPad T440p build with EDK2 and SMMSTORE, then we extract that for insertion into other boards in a more generalised way via shim logic in include/fw/rom.sh.
  • Removed the fspcc36ae2b5775fa7400cb3282680afc0f6cb37a3c submodule in coreboot, used on Topton X2E N150. We now use the latest FSP, but this means breaking older builds when doing vendor injection. This is unavoidable.
  • Added a noconfig variable that can be set by build trees/targets, where they are multi-tree but no configs are used. This makes it appear under a fake name called noconfig, e.g. elf/grub/default/efi/noconfig/grub.elf when compiled.
  • get.sh: use -L in find command, because some projects now use symlinks to metadata from other projects to ensure rebuilds. For example, edk2 coreboot targets (dummy targets) rely on grub and seabios efi builds. When these builds have to change, we need to ensure that the edk2 coreboot build is re-done. Here, we mean the find command used for finding files to hash when checking whether a given project has changed in build system setup.
  • Properly sort submodules by directory name, so that recursive submodules can be handled in projects. This is in the submodule handling on get.sh.
  • get.sh: support arbitrary submodule config path, for projects that use multiple versions of a submodule. For instance, EDK2 uses multiple versions of brotli.
  • SeaGRUB removed; on boards that still have the coreboot-payload version of SeaBIOS and GRUB, we now only do images that have GRUB or SeaBIOS as the primary payload. SeaBIOS’s payload loading isn’t always reliable, and GRUB has improved its allocator considerably snice a few years ago. We also now use EDK2 on most boards, so testing GRUB is the minority of boards that still use it exclusively is much more feasible. This simplification is permanent, given that standalone SeaBIOS/GRUB are now obsolete; EDK2 is the preferred payload now, with EFI versions of SeaBIOS and GRUB spliced into the EDK menu for backward compatibility with older Libreboot setups.
  • Stronger use of make distclean on projects before building, made feasible due to Libreboot’s aggressive out-of-tree caching of project builds based on metadata checks in lbmk.
  • Allow noconfig=n on a project, which allows it to be multi-tree and use the same tree on different targets, even when build configs aren’t required; in some cases, configs are done exclusively in mkhelper settings. This is part of Libreboot’s decision to make all projects multi-tree, alongside allowing use of N upstreams per project instead of just one upstream.
  • Simplify release=n handling in lbmk; don’t execute mkhelpers. Skip source fetches if release=n, so that the corresponding source won’t be downloaded. This is necessary to exclude MrChromebox sources as well as builds in releases, because they aren’t ready for stable release in Libreboot yet.
  • init.sh: Portable date usage; git’s own date handling now used. We no longer rely on GNU-specific extensions to the date command, for git repository initialisation on release builds.
  • Allow running mk from outside the main work directory. The build system now changes work directory accordingly.
  • Enable 3-way-merge when running git am in get.sh - this enables easier updates on project revisions.

Config changes

  • Most boards still use CBFS or NVRAM option table (static option table, or modify CBFS). A few boards, like the HP EliteBook 820 G2 and Topton X2E N150, use SMMSTORE-based option config but it has not yet been set up in lbmk.
  • Set me_state to Disabled by default, tree-wide in coreboot (default tree). We already set the HAP bit in IFD anyway, but this is an extra layer of disablement, to make sure that the Intel ME is deader than dead.
  • Optimised GRUB modules; all FS modules now included, fewer errors shown in the GRUB shell at boot. Modules generally optimised to ensure that there is still not a lot of flash space used compared to the default upstream setup.
  • Added xxd to dependencies, needed by CSMWrap when making SeaBIOS EFI builds as it runs xxd -i on SeaBIOS CSM builds to create header files that are then wrapped inside CSMWrapper’s shim code.
  • Corrected the Dell OptiPlex 5050 DMI string code to say 5050 SFF, not 3050 Micro.
  • Don’t use dell.com as primary download mirrors in the vendor inject script. This reduces the number of download errors when people inject images that use deguard.
  • Scan all GRUB configs on all devices, without using fixed device lists in GRUB. Instead, asterisks are used. More BTRFS subvolumes are also checked, also via use of asterisks.
  • General cleanup on GRUB configs. Redundant features removed e.g. manipulation of gfxterm. The default setup works fine. GRUB never worked reliably for on serial output anyway and most modern computers don’t support any of the interfaces that GRUB supports in this context.
  • Added ImageMagick to dependencies (needed for EDK2 boot logo).
  • SMMSTORE enabled by default, on all targets that use EDK2 as a payload. This means that Libreboot users can now enter a standard setup menu at boot time, configuring their machines (e.g. boot order) in a way that is both persistent and does not require re-building the firmware.
  • Added 4MB and 8MB targets for KCMA-D8 and KGPE-D16 mainboards. This, along with use of the 15h.org fork of coreboot on these boards, for improved raminit and various bug fixes. It uses AMD AGESA source code instead of the custom source code written by Raptor Engineering. The modified AGESA code has better CPU and memory initialisation, supporting more hardware combinations and it supports higher amounts of RAM.

  • Fully export git author/commit date when re-initialising lbmk on release builds. This is done on every related git command, for deterministic operation.
  • Fam15h coreboot: patch out __unused variables and cast them to (void) instead, where unused, to prevent build errors in GCC 16.
  • Gentoo Linux dependencies setup added to lbmk.
  • Fix offline GRUB builds. The build system caches sources and repos, but GRUB had custom logic in it for downloading unversioned PO files from translationproject.org - so when I did my FOSDEM talk, my demo failed because the internet was down, while I wrongly believed I had everything cached. GRUB was modified to not download the files, and lbmk caches them instead. They are also now version-checked, by virtue of checksum; no versioning is actually provided upstream, but their contents were checked and further updates will inspect the diffs between them. Basically, whatever is on translationproject.org pertains to the current HEAD in GRUB. It’s fine because the way gettext works is that if a literal string is not defined, it defaults back to original language. In this context then, use of the wrong PO files will just result in some sentences not being translated. Still, a bug in the way the files are handled might allow for a… buffer overflow, on unversioned files that GRUB was downloading without checking hashes. Yes. Libreboot fixed this reproducibility problem by forking the repository containing the files, keeping it static. Next time I do a talk, my demo won’t fail. I fixed this literally a few hours after my talk.

Nvmutil changes

A lot of changes were made to util/nvmutil/ to the extent that it deserves its own release log:

  • Generally safer use of macros (use brackets).
  • Removed errno-based error handling. Just return zero or one, based on logical errors, but do not rely on the status of errno for error exits. Only use return values as appropriate to POSIX in libc functions. However, errno reset is handled more reliably accordingly, after return from libc functions; not required but also not counterindicated by POSIX. - dell-flash-unlock errno handling also fixed in the same way. We previously relied heavily on errno for exit, in ways that were not portable. Not all libc will properly reset it, and may set it randomly even when a given function logically returns with success. Any number of things could set it, so it’s not a reliable mechanism for general error handling.
  • Don’t use -pedantic flag - also remove this on spkmodem-recv. Reduces the chance of pedantic build errors based on warnings.
  • General correctness fixes; bound checks, proper handling of word alignment, use of uintptr when converting pointers, etc. The code is generally much safer, in terms of memory management, as a result of extensive auditing.
  • EINTR-safe wrappers for various functions; loop until EINTR clears, where error occurs, otherwise err-exist on non-EINTR errors. Properly ignore EINTR on close() if function returns with error (EINTR on close is not an error condition in POSIX, and the descriptor should be disregarded in such scenario).
  • More testing and fixes for OpenBSD, especially on memory management (much stricter libc in OpenBSD).
  • Generalised I/O functions for libc functions like read, write,preadandpwrite` - EINTR-safe, with stricter (than libc) checks against incomplete writes and such.

NOTE: This applies to the standalone version of nvmutil. There was an attempt to rewrite it in a much larger utility, mentioned in the following section about canceled changes for this release (see notes below about libreboot-utils).

Canceled changes

A few changes were worked on, but did not land in this release. They pertain to two major projects:

util/libreboot-utils

This was an extension of nvmutil that later became a generalised set of utilities alongside a library for handling things like atomic writes, and userspace mitigation against various types of TOCTOU attacks. Not really critical for nvmutil itself, but…

An attempt was made to implement a hardened version of mktemp called mkhtemp. It implemented several mitigations in userspace against TOCTOU attacks e.g. directory replacement and symlink attacks.

Check lbmk git log for util/libreboot-utils to see more (might have been util/libreboot_utils.

Mkhtemp was started when implementing atomic writes for nvmutil, but then I naturally made use of tmpfiles for that, and that led to me auditing every implementation of mktemp. I concluded that I could do better - and I did.

Examples of how mkhtemp innovated:

  • Still provided libc-like behaviour when requested, but:
  • Stricter checks against use of world-writeable non-sticky directories.
  • Generally stricter error-exit handling.
  • Relentless checks against changes to files during operation/check, inode changes and so on. Checking that a file wasn’t operated on by another program - basically, openat2-like security was attempted to implement in userspace, though openat2 was also enabled as a fast method on Linux.
  • Own implementation of rand, wrapping around Linux getrandom and BSD arc4random. It provided various functions for rand, including one that matched the semantics of arc4random_buf (rset function in libreboot-utils).
  • Descriptorless operation in general, on files and directories.
  • Pathless operation where possible - including userspace directory walking and sandboxing.
  • Unveil-like restrictions in userspace (and pledge/unveil usage in OpenBSD).
  • Use of symlinks disabled by default.

…it was an over-engineered piece of crap, and had several memory issues related to stack memory usage, which tripped up a lot on BSD. The could could be tidied up and finished, but I came to a conclusion:

Distros would never accept it. Mkhtemp worked fine on Linux, but it had much stricter operation that would trip up most build systems that use it. I tried it in lbmk to replace mkhtemp, symlinking it in PATH, but for example GRUB had virtually no error checking on mktemp. Most programs that use mktemp wrongly assume that it can never fail, so it doesn’t; implementations try to mitigate errors and continue operation, in ways that are extremely complex. Mkhtemp was a clean attempt at stricter TMPDIR usage.

Because I decided it was a waste of time, I don’t think I care to write more about it in this changelog. Check lbmk git log if you’re interested.

util/spkmodem-decode

A heavily extended version of util/spkmodem-recv that implemented much stronger noise protection, attempted automatic tone detection and frequency selection, plus more. I went a bit overboard with it and decided that it was an overengineering effort. It will not be resumed at any point. You can find it in lbmk git log. (might have been util/spkmodem_decode).

Pointless effort. Spkmodem the protocol is unusable in most setups regardless.

The most pointless effort ever, such as:

  • Edge detection along with amplitude, for more reliable operation on noisy signals
  • Recalibrate timing to signals periodically, adjusting for tone. The idea was ta allow for the tone separator to drift over time, and have our code adapt to subtle changes to reduce the amount of noise. Right now, spkmodem shows a lot of noise on poor signals.
  • A bunch of other equally useless changes.

Completely pointless. The simpler code works just fine, so the effort was abandoned and thus spkmodem-recv is still present; this is a cleaned up version of what was inherited from GNU GRUB several years ago.

When you accept AI, you become deskilled and you erode the trust that exists between you and your users. You remove the human connection between maintainers and users, and your project will start to become dependent on what is - yes - proprietary technology, paid for in blood. Even if that causes me to have to spend weeks integrating a totally new system to replace it. That is precisely, exactly and indubitably how far I will go to prove my point.

That is why I went to such extreme effort integrating EDK2. Rather than replace U-Boot with yet another incomplete UEFI implementation, I simply added EDK2 which is already feature-complete as it is the reference, industry-standard implementation of the UEFI spec.

CrabEFI was what I initially considered, to replace U-Boot. This is a new payload written by Arthur Heymans, and the project itself is excellent, but rustc/cargo is inherently unreliable for several reasons:

  • Unpredictable toolchain setup. Most people use e.g. rustup and they set up all sorts of custom environments. Much less predictive than e.g. LLVM/GCC provided in distros. Libraries and such are provided by Cargo, instead of distros, and users often leave everything out of date, leading to breakage.
  • Rust is not standardised; the specification is implementation-defined, and code written today may still compile in the future when the spec changes, but code behaviour would naturally change as a result of the latter.
  • Given the above, we would have to bootstrap rustc/cargo ourselves, and we would have to do it from source (from a compiler like GCC which already has source bootstrapping courtesy of the Guix project and others).

Rust is awesome, but in my opinion not production-ready yet. Give it another ten years. EDK2 is infinitely more complex, but the size of the code is not a concern as it is generally stable, and written in C (some small bits of it are in C++). It has the most amount of eyes on it, and regularly receives security audits. It’s one of the most battle-tested codebases on the internet, and works well.

CrabEFI will likely be merged in Libreboot at some time in the future, when Rust tooling has stabilised across distros (including BSDs). It has a much better design, even if it’s not yet feature-complete, and use of Rust means that it will have fewer memory bugs. For now, Libreboot uses EDK2 to replace U-Boot and it has been enabled by default on all boards.

On memory safety, we can say contrarily that EDK2 is at least stable; bugs are also stable. That’s the point. We have stable C/C++ compilers, properly tested according to formalised standards (not really, because GCC and LLVM do all sorts of whacky things too, but they also try to be compatible with each other behaviourally). You want your code, when compiled, to behave exactly the same, bugs included. This is more strongly guaranteed with projects written in C and C++ (especially pure C projects, and most of EDK2 is in fact pure C).

It was originally intended that U-Boot would become Libreboot’s primary payload on x86, but alas. I bit the Intel-flavoured bullet and went with EDK2.

Errata

EDK2 issues

No ability to change the keyboard layout yet - a graphical menu option can be added for this later in EDK2, saved to SMMSTORE. The EFI build of GRUB uses terminal_input console only, and input is thus handled by the EDK2 input drivers (ditto USB mass storage and other storage devices); GRUB’s nativedisk driver is removed for example, and its native NVMe/xHCI drivers are no longer needed as in previous Libreboot releases.

EDK2 input drivers work with both USB and PS/2 keyboards in Libreboot. GRUB is made to use console input instead of at_keyboard as it otherwise lacks USB keyboard support in the EFI build. Thus, layouts must be handled by EDK2. There is code for this in EDK2, not currently handled by either Libreboot or MrChromebox so it all defaults to UK QWERTY in this release. Upstream (MrChromebox) uses US QWERTY by default, but Libreboot is a British project, so EDK2 was patched accordingly. Work will be done post-release.

Keymapped images no longer provided. There is now only one ROM image per config on each mainboard. This simplifies builds, and users can insert a keymap.gkb file inside CBFS from config/data/grub/keymap/ if they wish; if you add a grub.cfg to flash with terminal_input set to at_keyboard, this will work on devices with PS/2 keyboards if wanting to use the GRUB EFI payload (a command in grub.cfg to load the keymap is also needed, specifically keymap (cbfsdisk)/keymap.gkb.

EDK2 has been tested extensively on all Intel hardware from GM45 e.g. ThinkPad X200/T400, all the way to Intel Kabylake hardware supported by Libreboot e.g. ThinkPad T480, X280, Dell Optiplex 3050/5050.

Want old GRUB/SeaBIOS back?

The new compatibility modules in EDK2 should more than suffice for most users, who may still want GRUB/SeaBIOS for booting their existing Linux and BSD setups. It is recommended that you convert these to EFI or just reinstall them - use of UEFI is strongly encouraged as the default from now on, but Libreboot must (will) continue supporting older setups.

FreeBSD users booting with SeaBIOS text mode may be interested in this, as BIOS-mode FreeBSD bootloaders do not boot with anything else. A UEFI-based FreeBSD installation will work just fine in EDK2 though, so new FreeBSD installations are best recommended via EDK2 (do not use the compatibility modules of GRUB/SeaBIOS).

Some users might want it. Here are some brief notes. They won’t be added to the main documentation as they pertain to a configuration that Libreboot now regards as obsolete, but some users may nonetheless find it useful in the short term:

Older mainboards that are 32-bit only or with limited flash space still use the standalone GRUB/SeaBIOS payloads without EDK2; some newer ones with weird graphics setups also still use lone SeaBIOS/GRUB e.g. HP EliteBook 8560w.

To re-enable use of standalone GRUB/SeaBIOS (without edk2), modify target.cfg as follows for your board: remove build_depend, payload_edk2 and grubtree variables. Then add these lines:

payload_grub="y"
payload_seabios="y"
payload_memtest="y"

This is obsolete now in Libreboot and may even be removed in a future release. EDK2 is much better as it boots nearly everything, and supports more hardware setups. It is simply much more versatile than Libreboot’s old setup as in the previous release.

Then you can just re-build. NOTE: In the above guidance, build_depend is assumed to be grub/default seabios/build memtest86plus/default by default. You may want to set them explicitly:

build_depend="seabios/build grub/default memtest86plus/default"

You may also wish to set the GRUB tree explicitly:

grubtree="default"

Example config: config/module/coreboot/t480_vfsp_16mb/target.cfg

Just do this and re-build if you want these old setups back. This will be supported for as long as feasible, but will probably be removed at some point, maybe years from now, maybe a week from now. Use it while it’s there. The xHCI patches are still in there, and everything is configured as it should be.

In setups with EDK2, please note: txtmode not provided. If wanting e.g. SeaBIOS txtmode, look at e.g.:

  • config/module/coreboot/t480_vfsp_16mb/config/libgfxinit_corebootfb

Renamed it to libgfxinit_txtmode in this example and do:

./mk -m coreboot t480_vfsp_16mb
./mk -s coreboot t480_vfsp_16mb

In the menu that appears, go into Devices -> Display -> Framebuffer mode and select Legacy VGA text mode - this is not recommended for any new setups, but the FreeBSD bootloader starts in text mode and the framebuffer modes in coreboot can’t switch back to it. Booting in text mode is recommended when booting the FreeBSD BIOS-mode bootloader, and then FreeBSD can be set up for KMS in Xorg/Wayland. Otherwise, new installations should be done in EFI mode directly via EDK2 (no compatibility modules). More information about this is available in Libreboot’s BSD documentation.

CSMWrap errata

CSMWrap is the SeaBIOS CSM build provided inside EDK2. It hogs an entire CPU core at boot, so e.g. quad-core will show up as three-core inside Linux. It’s a known limitation that will be corrected in a future release, due to the design of CSMWrap. If you need backward compatibility, it’s better to use the GRUB EFI build instead which does not have this problem. Both GRUB EFI and SeaBIOS CSM are available in the EDK2 menu via ESC keypress at boot time.

Users are best served just switching to native UEFI boot with ESP, using Libreboot’s EDK2 payload.
