item.title: AI was great until it was not (108 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://thetheorygirlie.substack.com/p/ai-was-great-until-it-was-not, See on Hacker News

When I arrived at Oxford, I experienced what many would call a cultural shock. Beyond the flamboyant parties and visible micro-aggressions of the gowned elite, my physics and math courses felt radically different than before. The lectures were significantly more impersonal; the professors were a bit hostile; the crowd was huge, and everyone had something to prove. This would have felt rather normal if I had decided to continue my education in Argentina, but, instead, I had adapted to the American education model—at a school like Northwestern no less, which had a fairly small physics program. Not only that, I spent half of my undergraduate education surrounded by PhD students, taking the same classes as them.

But a masters in England was different. It felt bigger, more ominous. Most people opted to study and solve problem sets alone, and when we tried to work in groups there was an expectation to perform as the “genius” type. I had PhD offers from Harvard and Oxford straight from undergrad, and I felt like I had to prove I deserved it. It was partly my fault. I did feel the need to brag in order to be taken seriously, but it backfired on me. It was awkward at first, but the environment shifted drastically mid Michaelmas term. Pretty soon our discussions and ego games shifted from meaningless whiteboard debates to my classmates simply stating “I just asked ChatGPT how to do it.”

ChatGPT?

This was in late 2024. I had heard of AI in the past. Everyone was raving about it all year, but no one I knew had used it for class. I saw people complaining about how much water it used, how terrible it was for the environment and a few people even stated that it might kill us all someday. This felt like complete nonsense to me. I recall when I was writing my undergraduate thesis in mid-spring. I opened instagram to procrastinate for a few minutes, and I saw a popular “PhD influencer” (whatever that means) say she put her name in ChatGPT, and it blasted a lot of information about her and how great she was. I thought it was a bit scary for a “website” to pull up all your information like that (and I found the endeavour a bit narcissistic), but I was deeply curious, so I gave the chatbot a chance. I remember asking some question about scattering amplitudes, and it replied with nonsense. So, I pressed it and asked again with more detail, and it said:

“You should ask a theoretical physicist.”

And at that point, that was enough for me to close the window and never open it again.

That is, until a few months later, I was studying at Oxford with my “friends” at the time, and they kept raving about how ChatGPT could do their homework. Problem sets for most of the MMathPhys courses at Oxford are not graded. Real grades come from exams or your dissertation. A few classes require you to submit homework, but ‘passing’ is enough. I thought it was a bit meaningless to ask a chatbot to do everything for you when the entire purpose of the homework was to serve as exam practice. Yet, in January 2025, I found myself stuck trying to solve one QFT question, so I asked the chatbot like my friends recommended, and, again, it said some bullshit. I didn’t look at it again until a few months later.

It was a bit odd how the idea of “homework” had seemed to decay. Before, at least, we had the decency to look at Stack Overflow, and scout for similar problems or problem solving techniques that could help, but now suddenly people weren’t even doing that. They just asked ChatGPT to do everything. It defeated the purpose of doing homework to be honest. Though, I think we had lost that a while ago. I always thought that beyond practicing for the exam, problem sets were great to learn what collaboration during problem solving is like.

But in reality, collaboration has rarely been part of my reality as a student. The last time I recall truly collaborating with fellow students was in my freshman year of college. I was taking multivariable calculus with a bunch of engineering students. I knew two girls, Andrea and Juliana, from orientation and we immediately formed a small group chat to work together. We would try each problem set separately first, and then each of us would send our answers to the group chat and we would debate. For instance, one girl would ask me “oh, that’s a clever way to do this question. How did you know we had to integrate over this curve? Can you explain it to me?” or tell me “Hey, I think this question is wrong! You should use Lagrange multipliers this way instead.” And I would do the same thing for them. I learned a lot in that class, and I partly owed it to my great collaborators at the time. Debating, discussing and just learning from them was genuinely lovely. It helped me become better at math and truly grasp all the concepts.

I was deeply excited to start the physics major and collaborate with other physics peers. In the fall term of my sophomore year, I signed up for an honors differential equation math class with a friend who was also a physics major. As I thought was customary, we sent each other our solutions to check. It was my first time taking an honors math class, while that friend had taken three before. I also had to miss the first two lectures since my academic advisor insisted I wasn’t ready for honors, and I spent a week on a deeply boring standard class before I convinced the professor to let me switch. That is to say, I made a ton of mistakes in that first homework. So I messaged my friend like I had done in past and started asking: “Oh, it seems I misunderstood this concept, what do you mean here? Why is this true? I missed this class, so I thought we had to do something different” to which she accused me of trying to plagiarize her work and started ignoring me completely, and telling other people I was trying to copy her. Our friendship was never the same after that. And I learned a difficult lesson: I was alone. For the rest of the course, I worked on homework alone, I studied for exams alone, and I ended up with an A in the class. Actually, I spent most of my degree working alone, even as an undergrad among PhD students. I would explain my answers to my classmates, but I rarely had that back and forth from freshman year again.

That being said, ChatGPT just made the environment surrounding collaboration more bleak. Now, there was nothing beyond “Just ask ChatGPT.”

I was still hesitant to use AI. I saw many people in the MMathPhys use it for not only their homework, but for their dissertations and the research they expected to publish. I was confused. Another friend started using it as a therapist. I was still deeply confused. I was repelled by how agreeable it was, but it did give the weird illusion of having someone behind the screen.

Regardless, in May of 2025, all my bad decisions caught up to me. I actually spent most of my time at Oxford doing nothing. I always considered attending lectures some sort of social ritual. They have never helped me. I have always learned from books. Similarly, some problem sets were dense, uninsightful and useless, and if they were not needed for my grade, I wasn’t bothered to do them. I also had a PhD offer waiting for me at Harvard, so there was truly nothing to lose. I instead traveled a lot, went to parties, embarrassed myself, read a ton of books, played chess, fed the ducks and cried a lot. But at some point, I realized I had to get my masters degree and I had a month and a half to learn four Oxford MSc classes from scratch and pass my exams. I was cooked.

And there was ChatGPT. The thing about ChatGPT is that, well, it’s not a person. It doesn’t “think” like we do. But I realized it was very useful for one thing: rearranging what humans said in a more digestible way. So, I would sit with my cosmology and general relativity notes, and every time I got stuck or I couldn’t visualize a definition, I would just screenshot or copy the small section or sentence I did not understand and ChatGPT would re-explain it to me. Sometimes it included a quick example that helped me navigate index notation, for instance, or it would explain to me that torsion-free just meant that parallelograms closed.

One of the main incompatibilities with standard physics/math education and the way I think about problems is that definitions and derivations in a vacuum are a bit useless to me. I can follow complicated math and I can understand what a definition says, but it won’t click for me until I see a real illustrative example. This is not just a me thing. This is how Feynman thought about physics as well1, and I am sure a lot of people share this cognitive profile.

But instead of dealing with peers that got irritated at me and my stupid questions, ChatGPT provided that bridge almost instantly and with no fuss. After three weeks of using it, I realized I didn’t need it as much anymore. I could follow advanced concepts—like Penrose diagrams or Kerr Black Holes—on my own, make my own illustrative diagrams and derivations without AI. I took my exams two weeks after that. I learned the content General Relativity I&II, Cosmology and Geophysical Fluid Dynamics in a month and a half from scratch, while also taking the two Standard Model courses and a QFT in curved spacetimes class. My grades were between high passes and merits, but it was enough! I got my degree. And these were fully closed booked exams, so I did the work myself. But ChatGPT really helped me accelerate my knowledge acquisition.

That being said, I did not trust it at all for new research. Once I arrived to Harvard, I was given my first PhD project in early November of my G1 year, which is a bit early though not rare for high energy. I was working with a postdoc, and I was pleasantly surprised to see that the skills I learned in undergrad from my two mentors were incredibly useful for that problem. I embedded some twistor theory and chiral algebras into a nice mathematica notebook, which helped with a lot of calculations. I barely used AI on that project. It helped me find background literature and interpret some paragraphs/derivations in those papers. Beyond that, I only used Claude Opus to patch one piece of code in my library to help me deal with poles and residues in an expression because I wasn’t sure how to do it. That was it.

However, the single minus paper really changed the expectations surrounding AI in physics. Now, an internal model of OpenAI had found something researchers tried to work out for months before. That was cool, but it had nuance. A lot of the heavy lifting of that paper and the conceptual leaps were done by real people, but the accomplishment of AI was not to be understated. It was impressive. The proof was impressive and not straightforward, and this paper opened a lot of research directions in Celestial Holography. AI is actually great at proving things within a given framework. It’s also good at things that follow a strict logic or providing complex mathematical structures that are sound, but that’s not all that physics is. Or, I like to believe so.

The issue is that every time I showed my little mathematica notebook that I have coded mostly myself looking at the Wolfram documentation, both my seniors and PhD peers just would ask:

“Can’t ChatGPT do that?”

Maybe. But coding a problem in mathematica is not just about “efficiency” or writing fast code. It is about encoding a theory, a framework, working with corner cases, and learning. Maybe I could have asked Claude or ChatGPT to make a chiral algebras mathematica library, and it might have been good or better than mine, but then what would be the point? Maybe it would have been faster, slightly faster. Maybe I could have fed it all the different things I wanted to do, and let it code on the background and spit a ton of answers… but as a first year student that seemed to defeat the entire purpose of doing research in the first place. Furthermore, ChatGPT is not infallible. It can be very wrong. And not noticing when it’s wrong is just embarrassing for everyone involved.

I don’t believe in the grind of doing a difficult integral or proof from scratch to prove you are man enough to handle it (if a calculator or mathematica can do it, why suffer?), but I do think there is something valuable is solving an interesting problem, understanding a structure, and doing most of the conceptual heavy lifting. I finished my first project with very limited AI use, and the paper was published.

But when it was time to start my second project as a fresh G2, I did notice the environment had changed drastically. If you walk across the Harvard physics department and lean into the offices, a lot of people will have ChatGPT, Codex, Claude or similar open in their monitors. A lot of the emails I started to receive contained AI generated notes or notes based on ideas given by ChatGPT. It wasn’t just me, a lot of my peers go through this too, here and everywhere. This is a common experience now. Now, “brainstorming” means talking to ChatGPT. A lot of my time is spent deciphering ChatGPT notes, realizing it’s nonsense, and moving on to the next.

I was annoyed. I had objections, questions, and concerns, but I was shut down and told to ask ChatGPT. So, I asked ChatGPT and it just “validated” everything I said, but didn’t propose any solutions. The problem is that I wanted to debate with my superiors, ask questions… and I couldn’t. I realized a lot of doing a PhD in theoretical physics is dealing with loud people screaming at a blackboard, so it doesn’t feel very interactive either. Some people say a lot of fancy words. Bullshitting is common practice some say. I realized at some point that it wasn’t just me; there was some posturing, some performance, and ChatGPT made that worse. So, I was alone with a chatbot again. But, now, I didn’t have a set of lecture notes written by a top physicist at Cambridge about a theory that was established almost a century ago… I had a couple of papers, vague ideas, and nowhere to go because on a PhD you work out things no one has done before.

And it wasn’t good. Because I am just a second year PhD student and I don’t know anything. I know a lot of things, but in the grand scheme of things, I am inexperienced and I need mentors. And a chatbot cannot be my mentor. And then I realized that same tool that helped me so much a year ago was drowning me and my field. I don’t think technologies are evil, but I do think how humans utilize some technologies can be harmful. But it’s not AI’s fault, it’s ours.

I did realize early on that a lot of people in my field were less focused on finding the truth than they were on projecting, being right and showing off. I realized early on that for a lot of physicists teaching and mentorship is more of a burden than something they deem particularly valuable. We want the fastest PhD students, the ones that published three papers in undergrad, the ones that finish a calculation the fastest. We want the hottest topics and the most citations. But if a chatbot can replace a PhD student, if it’s faster, more efficient and it can absorb Weinberg’s QFT volumes in five minutes, why do we need students at all?

Why do we collaborate when we can just work alone with a bot?

Remember when I mentioned I had that group chat with my engineering friends and we were constantly comparing and brainstorming? Sometimes, they would catch a concept or see a clean solution I didn’t notice, and I would do that for them too. That helped us grow, and it gave me a deep understanding of a lot of those concepts. I would solve exams in unexpected ways, but that was fun! It helped truly grasp the math and how beautiful it was. But that was also a healthy collaboration. It wasn’t about getting the highest grade, or having the smartest solution, gatekeeping or screaming. We would sit down, try it out, politely discuss, and explain. We wouldn’t be mean or condescending, we would just learn from each other and improve each other.

People keep us in check. Each person is different. We all have a different background, a different way of seeing the world. We come from different training. But, you learn from others and they learn from you too.

And we are losing that now too. Should we fear that colleagues working in AI companies might take our prompts and try to get ahead to solve a problem before we do? Should we fear for threats? Should we fear that our days as PhD students will be spent telling a machine to “try harder” instead of deeply understanding something new?

Truth is, I was very impressed and excited about how ChatGPT helped me study. Would I rather have responsive professors, lecturers that know pedagogy, physicists that want to write understandable papers instead of purposefully burying insight in meaningless jargon, and peers I can talk to without having an anxiety spike? Yes. I would rather have that one hundred percent. And I fear that now, it’s all going to be worse. Because we now have in our hands a machine that validates all of our biases and buries them in dozens of pages of meaningless math.

I am just a PhD student who feels a little defeated, not because AI might take my job, I am privileged enough for that to not be a concern (and let’s be honest, I am privileged enough to have the opportunity to do a PhD in theoretical physics). But because the way we are using AI is destroying what made science fun in the first place. Is it really fun to publish thirty papers in a week using AI just for the sake of it? One of my friends in the program rightfully asks “Are those papers worth publishing?”

The entire point of solving an interesting problem or understanding the mysteries of the universe is not to win an award or have the most citations, but to get closer to that almost mythical thing we call truth, to know the universe and ourselves through the study of the nature of things.

The problem is that the little chatbot in our pockets is making us more isolated and in so, it’s making us stray further from this humble goal: to learn. But it wasn’t just the chatbot, it was the culture around academia too. I think chatbots are a mirror, a deeply validating sycophantic mirror with the knowledge of the internet. But mirrors can be dangerous if we stay for too long too charmed by our own reflection, and we forget about everything and everyone else too. In particular, it would be pretty sad to destroy one of the few things that makes our life meaningful, not the fancy prize or the fancy position, but simply having a community to share and discuss and learn. To learn things. That is a beautiful thing.

-Nia

"If men could only see the cause, and why
This mountain of distress weighs down the mind,
They’d drop all else and study to find out
The Universe’s Nature and its layout—
Since it’s our status for eternity
That is at issue here, and not just one
Brief hour—the state in which all mortals must
Spend time to come, when once our days are done."

-Lucretius2

item.title: Overdose Offsets: Why Every Bag of Fentanyl I Sell Is Net Life-Positive (119 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://morewrong.lol/?post=overdose-offsets-why-every-bag-of-fentanyl-i-sell-is-net-life-positive, See on Hacker News

I sell fentanyl six days a week under the El at Kensington and Somerset, and every bag I sell is net life-positive. Each bag carries a small but real chance of killing whoever buys it. Each bag also sends $1.80 to the Against Malaria Foundation, which GiveWell estimates saves a child’s life for about $5,500. My customers die at a rate of roughly one per 4,000 bags. Four thousand bags at $1.80 buys nets for 1.3 children. Every death on my corner is offset, with a third of a toddler left over, and I’d like that number in the conversation the next time somebody calls me a murderer out the window of a passing Kia.

I arrived here the way most people in effective altruism arrive at their careers: by asking where my comparative advantage was largest. I spent four years as a quantitative trader at Jane Street. I was good, but I was replaceable, and so was every dollar I made there. Earning to give tells you to take the highest-paying work you can stomach and donate the difference. I took the Giving What We Can pledge in 2019. I have simply taken the “highest-paying” half more seriously than the people who sign it between sessions at EA Global. My customer base is the most price-inelastic in North America, my overhead is a fanny pack, and my plug in Fairhill has never once asked me to attend an offsite.

The question critics refuse to ask is not whether a bag can kill someone. Of course it can; that’s the product. The question is the net change in lives per bag:

ΔL = D/G − p

D = donation per bag ($1.80)
G = GiveWell cost per life saved (~$5,500)
p = probability a given bag is fatal (~1/4,000)

D/G comes to 0.000327 lives. p comes to 0.00025. Every bag nets about +0.00008 lives. In 2025 I moved roughly 21,000 bags, which my model attributes to 5.3 deaths in Kensington and 6.9 lives saved in Malawi, for a net of +1.6. My old desk at Jane Street saved zero lives on net, and nobody there ever had to step over anyone to get to work.

People object that the deaths in Kensington are real and the lives in Malawi are statistical. This is scope insensitivity with a zip code. A child dying of malaria in Lilongwe is exactly as dead as a man nodding out on the Allegheny steps, and arguably more tragic, because she wasn’t dopesick first. If you feel the Kensington death more vividly, that’s a fact about your eyes, not about the moral universe.

If I leave the corner, Hector from Lehigh Avenue has it inside of an hour. Hector sells the same tranq dope at the same price, with zero offsets and a pit bull named Dollar. The counterfactual to me is not “no fentanyl at Kensington and Somerset.” It’s fentanyl without malaria nets. Every person who wants me gone, including Officer Ruiz, who arrested me in August and asked whether I understood what I was doing, is functionally campaigning for Hector. I told Ruiz I’d modeled it extensively. He did not want to see the model.

I hedge under moral uncertainty, as Will MacAskill recommends. I keep Narcan in the fanny pack and hand it out with every bundle the way airlines hand out pretzels. If I see somebody go blue on my block, I hit them with it, and I book that as direct work, separate from the offsets. I hand out fentanyl test strips too. My product tests positive every time, which is more honesty than you’ll get from a Wawa hot dog.

This summer I began stamping my bags EFFECTIVE in red ink. Every serious corner has a stamp. Mine is the only one that’s also a mission statement.

Longtermists have taught us to weigh not just the life saved but the future that life makes possible. A girl under a net in Malawi has, in expectation, sixty years ahead of her, children of her own, grandchildren, and descendants across a future that may hold trillions of people. A 46-year-old man nodding on the steps of the Somerset station has, with respect, a shorter and less branching future. Weighted by descendants, I’m not trading one death for 1.3 lives. I’m trading a cul-de-sac for a family tree.

Sam Bankman-Fried’s mistake was operational, not philosophical. He was right that a serious altruist goes where the money is. He went to crypto. I went to the El.

My mother, who paid for Haverford, says she didn’t raise a drug dealer. That’s accurate. She raised a quant, and the quant made a lateral move.

People say I profit from addiction. Every job profits from something. Jane Street profited from the volatility of Robinhood users’ retirement accounts. At least my customers get high.

The strongest objection is that I could donate without selling. I could, but I’d be donating a Wawa cashier’s salary, which buys about half a child a year. I’d be keeping my hands clean at a cost of more than a child per year in Malawi. That isn’t ethics. It’s a skincare routine.

Last month a man named Darnell died on the steps of the Allegheny station with one of my bags in his pocket. I had already wired his $1.80 to AMF on the first of the month. Somewhere in Malawi a child is sleeping under a net because of Darnell, and I don’t think anyone in Kensington has ever said anything that nice about him.

item.title: LFM2.5-24B-A2B: Built for fast on-device agents (262 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.liquid.ai/blog/lfm2-5-24b-a2b, See on Hacker News

Today, we release LFM2.5-24B-A2B, a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device. It is the largest and final model in the LFM2.5 family, which now spans two orders of magnitude: from LFM2.5-230M to LFM2.5-24B-A2B.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B is competitive with Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, a model with ~50% more total and active parameters, on five of eight agentic and tool-use benchmarks, scoring 48.09 on LiveClaw versus 38.19 and 27.69 on AutomationBench versus 8.72.  Because only 2B parameters are active per token, it runs up to 1.7× faster than comparable MoEs on-device, with 184 tokens/s on an Apple M5 Max and up to 21K output tokens/s on a single NVIDIA B300 GPU.

The base (LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base) and post-trained (LFM2.5-24B-A2B) models are open-weight and available today on Hugging Face and our Playground. Check out our docs on how to run and fine-tune it locally.

What changed since LFM2-24B-A2B

LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on our previous LFM2-24B-A2B release, with an expanded vocabulary and context window, scaled-up pretraining, and large-scale reinforcement learning. Unlike its predecessor, LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a reasoning-only model that produces an explicit chain of thought before its final answer. We adopted this strategy to leverage its high decode speed and improve answer quality.

Architecture. It keeps the 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA. The two architectural changes are the context window extension from 32,768 to 131,072 tokens, and the in-place tokenizer expansion, which doubles the vocabulary from 65K to 128K tokens for better non-Latin tokenization.

Pre-training was scaled up from 17T tokens to 33T tokens.

Mid-training has two phases. The first runs 2T tokens at 32K context on curated, higher-quality data weighted toward reasoning, math, code, instruction following, and multilingual text. The second runs 300B tokens at 131K context, weighted toward long context data. Tool calls and multi-turn trajectories appear throughout both phases to prepare the model for agentic workloads.

Post-training turns LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base into the agentic LFM2.5-24B-A2B in a five-stage pipeline as illustrated below: (1) Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), (2) Teacher Specialization, (3) non-agentic and (4) agentic Multi-Domain On-Policy Distillation (MOPD), and (5) Agentic Reinforcement Learning (Agentic RL), training the model inside agent harnesses, such as OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, Pi, and OpenCode.

During teacher specialization, LFM2.5-24B-A2B exhibited well-known reward-hacking behaviors: searching for the final answer in a repository's git history or on platforms like GitHub, PyPI, and Hugging Face. More surprisingly, it even figured out it was in a sandbox, as shown in the examples below.

This behavior looks emergent but might be explained by training data containing similar patterns. We tightened our sandboxes in response, and all reported results below come from sealed evaluation environments.

Benchmarks

We evaluated LFM2.5-24B-A2B across 16 benchmarks covering tool use and agentic workflows, knowledge, instruction following, math, and coding. Despite being the smallest model in total and active number of parameters, it is competitive with, and often outperforms, larger MoEs with ~50% more total and active parameters, such as Qwen3.6-35B-A3B.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B leads or matches the competition on five of the eight tool-use and agentic benchmarks (AutomationBench, BFCLv4, ToolSandbox, LiveClaw, and τ³-Bench Banking), with its widest margin on AutomationBench, where it scores more than three times the next-best model. It also leads on all three instruction-following benchmarks. Larger models keep an edge on knowledge-heavy benchmarks like GPQA Diamond, HLE, and AA-Omniscience, and on coding benchmarks like SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode) and SciCode.

The results make LFM2.5-24B-A2B an ideal foundation for agents that need to reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device. For knowledge-heavy workloads, we recommend pairing LFM2.5-24B-A2B with retrieval or web search, which plays to its tool-calling strength.

Fast inference everywhere

LFM2.5-24B-A2B ships with day-one support across the inference ecosystem:

  • llama.cpp — GGUF checkpoints for efficient edge inference
  • MLX — Optimized inference for Apple Silicon
  • vLLM — GPU-accelerated serving for production throughput
  • SGLang — High-performance GPU serving framework
  • ONNX — Cross-platform inference across diverse accelerators

All runs were collected on Pipette, the same benchmarking infrastructure behind Liquid AI's public device performance data.

Edge inference. Due to the efficient LFM2 architecture, LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest of the compared MoEs at reading in prompts and generating answers. It decodes 184 tokens/s on an Apple M5 Max and 114 tokens/s on an AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395, up to 1.7x faster than the next-best model, while using the least memory.

GPU inference. To demonstrate the competitiveness of LFM architecture we compare the GPU inference throughput to other similarly sized MoE models. We measure GPU throughput (total output tokens / wall time) on a single NVIDIA B300 GPU using a sustained-load setting: at each concurrency level, we continuously maintain the target number of in-flight requests, replacing each completed request immediately.

We benchmark each model with SGLang 0.5.22, 1,024 input tokens, up to 256 output tokens, in BF16. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest model in its size class, reaching over 21K output tokens per second at high concurrency.

Run local agents with LFM2.5-24B-A2B

LFM2.5-24B-A2B’s size, speed, and capabilities make it a great choice for agents that run continuously on your own hardware. item.title: We’re releasing Jev 1.14.0 along with experimental features for dreamers (319 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://typesafe.ai/blog/jev-1-14, See on Hacker News

TL;DR: We're releasing an improved Jev 1.14.0 along with experimental features for our dreamers: images, a new type, and longer context. Enter the danger zone at your own risk. 🔥

Our philosophy

A huge debate we’ve been having is on the balance between reliability and creativity.

To really care about the prod builders, we should be shipping models that meet our quality bar for intelligence and have been battle-tested to the limits of what we can do internally.

On the other hand, there’s no way that our team has a full understanding of what is needed to spark delight in the world and build sick sci-fi. We don’t want to impose our values of extreme reliability on those dreamers.

Our solution: share those dreamer-ready features under “danger zone” flags in our API headers. These are features that will be here to stay for future models, are (as far as we can tell) better than what exists out there, and will continue to get better by leaps and bounds. But as a warning, we think there is still way too much jaggedness for us to vouch for these for production use cases!

See these new capabilities as a continuation of what we’ve built over 2 years of stealth. They’re less ready for automation, but very fun to play with. They’re also an early glimpse into what we’re focused on making reliable enough to meet TypeSafe standards.

Composable Images

Not only are we enabling multimodality for future Jev models, we’re enabling it for the current Jev that you all know and love. Surprise: the Jev you all know and love (jev-1.13.0) was multimodal all along!

Image support is fully composable via a find-and-replace in assets. You can put them anywhere that our JSON interface supports: in the state, instructions, or even criteria! Play around with it, push the boundaries of technology, and let us know where Jev can improve.

As a warning, all models (Jev included) perform worse on multimodality over pure text. Breaking down questions into the simplest possible decompositions helps a lot.

TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Images: true

Check out docs: docs.typesafe.ai/go/images

Types Beyond Decisions

We’re introducing another new type as well: box. It returns a single bounding box - no type errors allowed. It’s our first type that’s not purely meant for smart-if statements, and is a preview for our explorations beyond simple decisions into what else System One Models can support.

We made huge leaps and bounds on this one recently, so we’re enabling this only for jev-1.14.0 (spoilers).

Check out docs: docs.typesafe.ai/go/box

Size does matter, apparently 💅

We’ve heard you loud and clear on context lengths. Jev actually supports a much longer context length than we’ve enabled in production. We chose to limit it intentionally because Jev, like all models, is less reliable on longer contexts, and this constraint encourages more effective usage patterns in prod.

We aren’t your parents though, so while we strongly recommend limiting context length, you no longer have to:

TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Long-Context: true

Check out docs: docs.typesafe.ai/models#context-length

Opt-in to help us

We love the community’s desire to help make models better! We’ve added an opt-in to allow you to help find model jaggedness with your queries. We will still not train on your queries, but this does make it easier for us to find issues and help debug your use cases.

jev-1.14.0

We’re also releasing a new version of Jev under jev-preview! Not meant to be flashy but instead be small, subtle improvements to everything. Most things should be a tiny bit better, but we expect the largest gain in multi-lingual support.

Model releases should generally also be strict improvements, but we’re well aware of how much developers hate updating their dependencies. jev-latest will be updated to jev-1.14.0 in a week. jev-1.13.0 will be available for a while. 

We intend to give 60 days warning before jev-1.13.0 is formally deprecated, and 30 days for jev-1.14.0. We’ll release a deprecation policy prior to this.

Measuring Intelligence

As you all know, we dislike public benchmarks. However, we have our own internal best guesses on how to measure the form factor of intelligence that matters most for developers. 

We’re trying something new out here: we’re going to treat you guys like adults and share this with you all.

Some nuance:

  • This measurement is our best guess and will continue to evolve. If ever we show you our internal numbers again, don’t expect them to be consistent.

  • Don’t believe it entirely. Always favor your own experimentation and evals with your use cases.

  • We’re including only open weight models because we guard our validation set very closely and are spooked out about the data policies of our model providers.

  • This is likely biased towards our models. Feel free to ignore our model, and instead focus on the relative ranking of open source models.

What’s next

Lots of people love to ask what kind of sci-fi we’re releasing next. While we are working on some mindblowing stuff, expect most releases to be beautifully boring (like we think AI should be): small improvements across the board, better stability, and features for real deployment.

item.title: OpenCode 2.0 (773 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://anoma.ly/notes/opencode-2-0/, See on Hacker News

OpenCode 2.0 is a major overhaul. It draws on millions of daily users' experience to deliver a system that can flex to everything an agent needs to be. There are quite a lot of new features, performance improvements, and bug fixes but here are some of the more impactful user-facing changes.

The Service

From the beginning OpenCode adopted a client/server model. However, this was not something it took advantage of by default and was mostly used by power users.

In 2.0 this server now automatically runs as a single background process on your machine. When you open up a TUI, the web interface or the desktop app they're all talking to the same central process.

If you're using the programmatic client @opencode/client to make your own scripts, they will autodiscover the local service and just work. This is particularly useful for scheduled tasks. You can also call it via CLI by using opencode api commands.

You can expose it to other hosts and run /pair or opencode pair to connect it to other applications. We have native apps in the works that take advantage of this flow.

The API

The old API grew haphazardly as we and the world collectively learned what agents are and should be. It was bad.

We started from scratch and examined all the weird use cases across the millions of users who use OpenCode every day. It now supports nearly anything you need to be able to do.

OpenCode is also aware of its own API and will call it to do useful things like moving the current session into a git worktree when starting new work.

We've also shipped a new client package @opencode/client that contains clients for vanilla JavaScript as well as Effect.

Code Mode

The models love to write code and OpenCode 2.0 takes advantage of that more than any other coding agent. We've built a minimal JavaScript interpreter in the @opencode/codemode package.

This package ingests MCP servers or OpenAPI endpoints, converting them into functions that the agent can call in a script. It can run these scripts natively without the complexity of Node.js VMs or embedding complicated solutions like QuickJS.

This lets your agent write scripts that can do things like call a tool, map over the results and call another tool. Single round trip instead of calling them one at a time.

All MCP servers in 2.0 are opted into codemode by default. This means you can add a thousand of them with minimal context bloat and your agent will discover and compose them to get things done.

Background Tasks

The latest batch of models are incredibly good at orchestration and it is important for harnesses to let them express the full extent of that capability.

First, we've added background subagents. This allows the primary agent to kick off some work to another one while it continues.

This happens automatically but you can also trigger it manually - even with a different model. It lets you do things like “spawn a background fable subagent to review this code” while you keep prompting.

Second, we've added background shell commands. The shell tool can be invoked asynchronously so long-running work does not have to block the primary agent. It'll be notified when things are complete.

If any foreground shell command or subagent takes longer than you expect, you can hit a hotkey to move them to the background so you can keep prompting.

Plugins

Although OpenCode 1.0 had a plugin system, it never got the attention it needed. To correct that, we forced ourselves to implement nearly every OpenCode 2.0 feature as an internal plugin and there are now 80+ of them. This guarantees that the Plugin API stays well maintained.

We've also promoted TUI plugins from experimental to stable. Since it is all powered by OpenTUI, you can build nearly anything. Here is an example of something useless.

We also spent quite a lot of time ensuring everything in OpenCode 2.0 can be hot-reloaded. So it can write a plugin for itself mid-session and use it right away - we covered the design of this in a previous blogpost.

You can ask OpenCode to build whatever plugin you want and it knows how to. But if you do want to read the docs, they are available here.

The SDK

OpenCode can also now be used as a library with the @opencode/sdk package. This is the exact same code that powers our CLI.

This means you can strip it down and make your own flavor of OpenCode that runs on a server or in specialized environments like Durable Objects. And then you can connect to it from any OpenCode client since it speaks the standard OpenCode server protocol.

It also has an optional Effect-based API.

This one is still in development as things are shifting but you can already use it.

Upgrading

To upgrade the CLI, make sure you're on the latest 1.x release, then run opencode upgrade --major.

To upgrade your desktop app, download the latest here.

There are some breaking changes.

1.0 plugins will not work in 2.0

Server API is completely different

tui.json config is moved to json

There are a lot of other changes but they are backwards compatible. It is worth pointing OpenCode at this doc so it can migrate things for you.

item.title: Anthropic's Scion is heavily inspired by Mononoke (398 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://sunshowers.io/posts/anthropic-mononoke/, See on Hacker News

Discuss on Hacker News or Lobsters.

Here is Anthropic describing (archive link) yesterday how their new version control system, Scion, uses a concept called “derived data” to make operations like blames more efficient:

Here is me, back in 2022, describing in my Oxide candidate materials how the Mononoke source control server I helped build uses a concept called “derived data” to make operations like blames more efficient:

I think the level of imitation goes well beyond having similar insights1. The fact that Sapling was only credited for “hard-won lessons”, and that Mononoke was not mentioned at all, borders on plagiarism. The post comes off as Anthropic claiming that Claude designed all this, while the reality is that our (extraordinary) team at Meta came up with many of the insights that Claude dutifully applied almost a decade later. (We looked at plenty of prior art for Mononoke and Sapling too, from Google’s SrcFS to write-ahead logs in databases.)

I am very glad that the vision our team had back in 2017-18 was so powerful and enduring — when you go against the grain, you’re always a bit unsure if what you’re doing is genius or madness, and I think Mononoke’s design has stood the test of time. And, to be clear, I do not have a problem with Anthropic copying Mononoke’s design. (This is part of why we put out open source — to benefit humanity through the spread of good ideas.)

But as LLMs continue to assist in designing new systems, they are likely to index heavily on existing designs. Mononoke is open source and in every LLM’s training set. If you ask Opus 5.5 or GPT-6 Astra (thanks Matthew Fowle) about prior art, they both immediately point out the similarities to Mononoke.

Giving credit to those that came before us is now easier — and more important — than ever. There is no longer an excuse.

item.title: Yandex outage: data shows that instead of going dark, malicious bots moved (274 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://blog.cloudflare.com/yandex-outage/, See on Hacker News

Following reported strikes on Yandex data centers, claims circulated on the Internet that Russian bot farms and influence operations had been knocked offline. HTTP traffic charts showed steep drops, fueling speculation that the infrastructure damage had stopped these malicious actors. However, aggregate traffic metrics can easily mislead. There are two autonomous system numbers (ASNs) associated with Yandex: AS13238 is used by Yandex’s search engine, while AS200350 runs its cloud services.

Using Cloudflare Radar and Bot Management data, we analyzed how these two ASNs were affected — and while both saw drops in traffic, they saw differing impact.

  • Yandex Search (AS13238): The drop in traffic consisted almost entirely of verified search crawlers indexing web pages, images, and site resources.
  • Yandex.Cloud (AS200350): There was a decline in malicious activities like vulnerability scanning and probing, but high-volume automation did not vanish — it simply migrated to other hosting providers.

While malicious traffic may originate from a particular provider, it does not necessarily tell us who is responsible for the traffic. Understanding why the strikes had little lasting effect on malicious traffic requires analyzing request behavior, rather than just overall traffic patterns.

What happened: the effect of the strikes and pre-event baseline

Between October 7 and 11, reported Ukrainian drone strikes hit three Yandex facilities in Russia, progressively knocking data centers and network capacity offline. As seen on Cloudflare Radar, this culminated in a near-total collapse of the Yandex network on October 11 when traffic plummeted to 99% below baseline for Yandex Search (AS13238) and 90% for Yandex.Cloud (AS200350). Despite a brief partial recovery, both networks remained disrupted through October 13, settling at 86-90% below normal baselines. (As of October 14 at 18:00 UTC, traffic is at 85% of normal.)

A drop in overall HTTP traffic only confirms that the network went down. It does not reveal whether malicious or evasive bots were disrupted. Looking at the pre-event automation baseline, we can see that before the strikes, automated requests accounted for 36.1% of all HTTP traffic observed globally across Cloudflare's network, and 35.8% of traffic from Russian IP addresses.

The outage had different effects on automated activity on the two affected ASNs because they served different roles.

Yandex Search ASN (AS13238) is used for search index crawling. Cloudflare classified 99.5% of its requests as automated, and 93.6% of its bot requests as Verified. Our analysis showed that traffic from this ASN indexed pages, rendered pages, and rendered images, which is consistent behavior for a search crawler. The Yandex Search ASN supplied about 7% of Russia-origin bot requests, and just 0.05% of the global total.

Yandex.Cloud ASN (AS200350) is a cloud-hosting network and carries a very different mix of automation. Approximately 95.0% of its scored requests were bots, but none of its observed bot requests were verified by Cloudflare. Yandex.Cloud’s bots looked more like software apps: nearly two-thirds of their requests sent data to websites, some identified themselves as JavaScript, Python, or Go programs, and a larger share went to software companies than Yandex’s search bots. The Yandex.Cloud ASN supplied about 2% of Russia-origin bot requests, and just 0.01% of the global total.

Impact of the event on overall bot traffic

"Bot traffic" refers to automated requests to websites on Cloudflare's network, such as crawlers and scripts, not necessarily activity on social media platforms. As Yandex’s networks lost capacity, their bot requests fell too. That was expected: nearly all traffic from Yandex Search and Yandex.Cloud was automated. While we saw the obvious drop in total traffic, we did not see any evidence linking a global disruption in malicious traffic to the drop in traffic from Yandex.

Russia-origin bot requests fell roughly in proportion to the Yandex traffic that went offline, since most requests from those networks were automated.

Impact on Yandex Search ASN (AS13238): less search crawling

The decline on Yandex Search ASN was almost entirely search crawling. Sampled requests showed that 78.1% belonged to verified YandexBot, 11.5% to YandexRenderResourcesBot, and 1.9% to YandexImages.

Among websites and services, the industry segment that saw the steepest drop was Publishing and Newspapers, where traffic from Yandex networks fell 44%. When the Yandex Search ASN went offline, customers simply saw less indexing from Yandex.

Impact on Yandex.Cloud ASN (AS200350): legitimate use and migrating malicious traffic

Yandex.Cloud displayed a completely different profile. Following the reported strikes, bot traffic from Yandex.Cloud fell about 40%. Several attack-like categories showed especially sharp declines. For example, WordPress plugin probing fell 90% and scanner-identified requests fell 93%. Interestingly (and tellingly), Cloudflare customer blocks on Yandex.Cloud traffic also fell 70% during the event period, suggesting that proportionately less malicious traffic was even hitting the Cloudflare WAF from this ASN.

The majority of traffic from the Yandex.Cloud ASN fell into two industry buckets: computer software and gambling. The computer software bucket was predictable for an ASN meant to host third-party applications and software integrations. In fact, we even saw that api.cloudflare.com is a top hostname for Yandex.Cloud request traffic. An overall majority of that traffic succeeded (requests returned 200s) both before and during the event, pointing to legitimate usage.

The gambling sector offers the clearest evidence that malicious automation relocated rather than disappeared. Nearly all of Yandex.Cloud’s bot requests were targeted at one gambling customer account, with traffic shifting among its hostnames. Immediately following the October 8 disruption, bot requests from Yandex.Cloud to this account dropped to zero. Simultaneously, identical requests began appearing from other Russian hosting ASNs, including Radist and Selectel. The incoming traffic maintained an identical fingerprint across providers:

  • The same JA4 TLS client fingerprint
  • The same uncommon request paths and HTTP headers
  • The same custom User-Agent strings

Overall, Russian bot traffic targeting gambling accounts remained essentially flat over the week, moving from 167.7 million to 170.1 million requests (+1.4%). The automation never stopped running; the operators simply migrated their workloads to alternate cloud providers once Yandex.Cloud became unavailable.

Across most industries, the share of bot requests from Yandex.Cloud returning any HTTP 4xx response fell. This is largely due to a drop off in the attack-like traffic mentioned above. This, in combination with the gambling customer analysis, shows that malicious traffic that was sending requests through Yandex.Cloud simply shifted its “services” to other providers after the service disruption.

Finally, when we analyzed social media traffic, we found no unexpected changes in traffic either from Russian-origin IPs (0.6% decrease in total traffic over the event period) or globally (1.2% increase in total traffic over the event period). We repeated the analysis on bot traffic hitting the “post”, “reply”, and “like” endpoints for a specific social media platform and similarly did not find an unexpected shift before or during the event period from either Russian-origin IPs (5.7% decrease in total traffic over the event period) or globally (1.1% increase in total traffic over the event period). Based on our assessment, the data does not appear to support the claims that the strikes crippled social media manipulation, though without further analysis with data outside of Cloudflare, we cannot conclusively say there is no connection.

What the data told us — and what it didn’t

When traffic from Yandex networks collapsed, speculation spread across the Internet that Russian influence operations and malicious botnets had suffered a crippling blow. Cloudflare data tells a different story: across Cloudflare's network, there was no evidence that the strikes knocked social media manipulation offline or otherwise disrupted malicious activity on the Internet. Instead, the data demonstrated:

  • Search indexing dropped. The overwhelming majority of the traffic that dropped from Yandex Search ASN consisted of verified YandexBot crawlers fetching news articles and web assets. The main impact was reduced content discovery in Yandex Search.
  • Malicious automation migrated instead of stopping. While vulnerability scanning and plugin probing temporarily dropped on Yandex.Cloud, high-volume operations quickly moved to alternative hosting networks.

A network disruption means that specific servers stopped sending requests, but it does not mean an automated threat disappeared. Cloud workloads are portable, so when a data center goes dark or an IP prefix gets blocked, operators can migrate their scripts to another provider in hours.

Our analysis here is a reminder that client ASN traffic volume is an unreliable proxy for interpreting automated bot behavior. Defending against automated threats requires inspecting request behavior, such as identifying shared JA4 fingerprints, monitoring anomalous request rates, and applying WAF rules to sensitive endpoints, regardless of which network the request originates from. Physical infrastructure is static, but malicious automation is built to move.

item.title: Fancy Curl Sites (137 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://nytpu.com/gemlog/2026-03-18, See on Hacker News

March 18, 2026 (Updated: October 14, 2026)

So a good while ago I added a fun curl version of my site, meant for viewing in the terminal. Try running these commands!

curl nytpu.com/gemlog/2026-03-18
# or
curl nytpu.com

(sorry Windows users, not my fault that ANSI escape codes are disabled-by-default in cmd.exe. And not my fault that in Powershell you have to use curl.exe instead of curl because Powershell inexplicably aliases that to Invoke-WebRequest.)

I posted about it a bit on the Fediverse, but otherwise didn't elaborate much on it becuase I figured it was fairly self-explanatory. But I've had a handful of people ask me how I did it, so I decided it might actually be worth it to write a post about how I did it (…like seven months late).

I should note this idea came from trinkey's (curl trinkey.com) and strongsand's (curl proot.party) curl sites, I didn't come up with it myself. Even though I did go about it quite a bit differently from them, all credit for the very cool idea goes to them. (UPDATE: unfortunately neither of their curl versions are functional anymore as of 2026-10-14.)

First, since it's the more interesting part, actually generating the ANSI-marked-up files to send to the clients. I entirely hand-wrote the index page and about page.

Note that I believe trinkey and strongsand generate theirs on-the-fly with the ratatui library (or similar), which is probably more convenient; hand-writing it seemed more expedient to me though.

I had the main escape code—ESC[, i.e. \x1b[—1 in a Vim register to easily paste when needed, and then the Wikipedia page for the main graphics codes open to reference the specific escape codes. And, yeah, that's about it. I experimented to decide on consistent styling I liked, and just referenced the Gopher version of my pages when crafting the marked-up curl pages.

Now, the notable thing about my version is that I have curl versions of the entirety of my blog, rather than just one or two pages being available. This is entirely due to a convenient coincidence: over four years ago I implemented outputting ANSI-marked-up plaintext in my custom markup language I use for my blog, Gemroff. Originally it was just to allow convenient previewing of drafts in the terminal while writing; but it was trivial to plug into my static site generator to immediately get Curl versions generated.

I did manually write a wrapper template for blog posts, as well as a template for the index page listing posts, but that plus a few extra lines in my static site generator was all that was needed to wire it up.

This is the main thing that makes it hard to say it's easy! since it was only easy for me because I use an entirely custom markup language and static site generator and I happened to make the right design choices years ago—e.g. my SSG also happened to already have support for multiple, modular output formats instead of solely HTML like other SSGs, since I tri-host my site on HTTP, Gemini, and Gopher.

However, offering nothing but a few hand-written pages for fun is a completely acceptable way to set up a site like this anyways, since it's just a neat gimmick and no one's likely to actually use it more than a few minutes of browsing.

Finally, the last step is actually presenting the Curl version of your site to any user agent containing curl, which for me was just a few changes to my Nginx config, with other servers it'd presumably be equivalently simple. The main feature I wanted was an override header (X-Original: true) so you could still get an unmodified HTTP response like someone casually running Curl likely wanted, and I wanted everything to be served statically still.

And… that's really it! As I said, when I first set it up it seemed fairly self-explanatory to me, but it is very non-orthogonal to what people normally do with either web servers or ANSI escape codes so I can see where people's curiosity/confusion came from. It would be neat to see more sites doing this trick around!

  1. EMDASH! AI-GENERATED! acksually I'll have you know that my markup language has had an explicit markup element for emdashes since November 2022. And believe it nor not: LLMs are trained on shit copied from actual authors, so LLMs wouldn't be using emdashes if they weren't already used in human-written works.

    And what, am I supposed to avoid having twenty parentheticals a paragraph, to where I feel the need to use emdashes to vary it up? Unthinkable! ↩︎

index
  • Back to top

I was diagnosed with squamous cell carcinoma in my mouth in May 2026. Here are some things I learned based on that experience so far.

  • You need to be doggedly persistent on scheduling things. Yes this means lots of phone calls. If you get an appointment a few weeks out, call back a few days later and ask for something sooner and see if they have any cancellations. I could only get an appointment 4 weeks out with an ENT (this was before I knew anything was wrong). My wife made me call back and I was able to get in that week due to a cancellation.
  • AIs may downplay the seriousness of things. I was chatting with various models and most pushed me in the direction of “you don’t have cancer” for a while. Just something to note.
  • You may need to push for comprehensive genetic testing. Some doctors were weird about this and didn’t order it promptly, even after telling me they would. My surgeon, who told me he’d get it done, eventually referred me out to an oncologist. This caused a multi-month delay to getting genetic results, since the first results were done on the surgery tumor, not the biopsy tumor. No one cares more about your case than you, so take control and send lots of follow-ups.
  • You can find the “Standard of Care” flow charts for every cancer type. Look and get through this yourself to see what the options are based on how things have progressed. NCCN guidelines. You may need to make an account, which you can do as a non-professional. I like the PDF files. They also have an interactive navigator. Use AI to help you figure out what to pick based on your case.
  • If surgery is recommended, I would try and talk to someone who has undergone the surgery. I did not do this and regret it. Ask them how intense things were, what it felt like, etc. My surgeon talked me through my surgery, but it was a lot rougher on me physically than I expected. Ask the surgeon how many of these surgeries they do a year and what the complication rate is.
  • Get a second opinion as soon as possible, no matter how much you like your plan. This may require a lot of calling and getting on an airplane, but I’d move to schedule it at a top cancer center as soon as you are relatively sure of your diagnosis. Ask for a second read of the pathology at the center where you get the second opinion.
  • I started a new folder on my Mac, and after appointments I’d dictate what happened and what the doctor said and have the AI make a new document summarizing things and asking its own follow-up questions for next time. Nice to be able to refer to this over time.
  • Check out all the resources and materials at the Sijbrandij Foundation. Sid (GitLab cofounder) took matters into his own hands when standard of care ran out. Schedule a call with these guys. They are great and have good materials and questions to ask your doctors.

Working from their 42,600-square-foot “multi-domain” secure facility that contracting documents say is authorized to handle Top Secret “sensitive activities” (SA), “sensitive compartmented information” (SCI), “special access program” (SAP) level information, offensive cyber operations (OCO), and “special technical operations” (STO), the 91st specializes in freezing out communications.

One document says that the squadron, and its Special Program Office, has the mission to “degrade, disrupt, deceive and exploit adversary telephony and information system.” It cut its teeth in Afghanistan, where it perfected “cellular coverage blackouts,” that is, the ability to shut down cellphone communications in a limited area.

Another unit operates a “malware lab” that collects together software and data from all sorts of adversary hacks and cyber operations, conducting analysis of “malicious artifacts,” and writing counter-software to thwart incoming attacks and implants.

An enormous part of the overall effort is “persona operations” — where soldiers and other literal keyboard warriors create false identities and fake internet addresses to operate in cyberspace without government attribution, to scout the web and surf social media, to engage individual users, and to do some influencing of their own.

Cyber Command’s (CYBERCOM’s) Joint Force Headquarters – Cyber, operating from its war room inside the National Security Agency-Texas facility in San Antonio, oversees Task Force Raider and other military election security efforts. Online support for Palestinians and opposition to Israel’s conduct in the Gaza war; vitriol against Donald Trump, or ICE, or the CIA and the FBI; or “disinformation” in general? None of these are a serious threat to our democracy. Yet somehow the federal government and the Pentagon have convinced us that they need to take extreme action, including controlling speech, to counter it.

What Americans see of military involvement in the election, they pretty clearly don’t like. When video circulated of DC National Guardsmen appearing in front of a ballot drop box, it quickly went viral, stoking outrage.

What people don’t see is that the military is also eyeing the vote in a much more systematic way in cyberspace. Why isn’t anyone asking what they are actually doing? And who is the actual target? Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev confirmed on Wednesday that there had been a fire at a facility of the Starlink satellite internet service near the capital Sofia last week.

Two young men holding German passports have been taken into custody in connection with the suspected attack, Bulgarian media later reported, citing investigators.

The satellite network is a strategically important part of Ukraine's defence in the war against Russia's invasion.

The fire had previously been made public by the pro-Western opposition alliance Democratic Bulgaria (DB). Radev said he would not provide any further details in light of the ongoing investigations.

According to DB, 11 of 17 antennas at a Starlink facility near Sofia were deliberately set on fire on October 9. The antennas were used in the war in Ukraine, DB said.

Pro-Western opposition parties said they suspected Russia was linked to the attack.

Two German passport holders in custody

Two men aged 20 and 21, both holding German passports, were detained in Bulgaria on Monday in connection with the suspected attack, several Bulgarian media outlets reported on Wednesday evening, citing investigators.

According to the news outlet Faktor.bg, the two suspects have migrant backgrounds and had legally entered Bulgaria from Greece through the Kulata border crossing.

The website reported that investigators were examining whether the suspects belonged to a larger sabotage network potentially linked to two men arrested in Germany earlier this week over a recent attack on a Starlink facility in Poland.

Sabotage suspected

Bulgarian officials stressed that the Starlink facility near Sofia was privately owned.

Bulgarian Interior Minister Ivan Demerdzhiev told parliament that additional security measures had been introduced at similar facilities, even though responsibility for their protection rested with their owners.

Plamen Tonchev, head of Bulgaria's State Agency for National Security (DANS), said he believed the fire at the Starlink facility was an act of sabotage.

"Such acts of sabotage cannot be ruled out in the future either," he warned lawmakers.

A fire also broke out at a Starlink ground terminal south of Warsaw on September 23.

Two suspected saboteurs accused of carrying out that attack in Poland were arrested on Tuesday in Nürtingen, near Stuttgart in south-western Germany.

The government in Warsaw suspects Russian intelligence services were behind the attack.

item.title: Banks are now trying to offload the AI data center debt they just underwrote (373 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://startupfortune.com/banks-are-now-trying-to-offload-the-ai-data-center-debt-they-just-underwrote/, See on Hacker News

JPMorgan, Morgan Stanley, SMBC and MUFG are quietly shopping pieces of the AI debt pile they helped build, a sign the lenders closest to the money have started hedging their own bet.

Six months ago, banks were racing each other to underwrite data center loans tied to Oracle, Meta and the rest of the AI buildout. Now some of the same banks are trying to get that debt off their books. JPMorgan, Morgan Stanley, SMBC and MUFG have been exploring significant risk transfers, according to a report from the Financial Times. These are deals that let a bank keep a loan on paper while shifting its riskiest slice to outside investors. The banks are doing this because they are bumping up against internal limits on how much AI-linked exposure any one lender can hold.

One case shows how stuck this has gotten. A group of banks including JPMorgan and MUFG has spent more than six months trying to distribute $38 billion in construction debt tied to a Texas and Wisconsin data center project leased to Oracle, Bloomberg has reported. Some lenders are now willing to sell pieces of it to non-bank buyers at a discount, just to move it. Six months is a long time to sit on debt nobody underwrote to hold forever.

Matthew Moniot, co-head of credit risk sharing at Man Group, told the Financial Times the deal sizes involved are "out of scale to anything we've thought about, ever." That is not a hedge-fund manager talking down a trade he wants no part of. It is someone whose job is pricing exactly this kind of risk, saying the numbers no longer fit any model he has used before.

Oracle is the clearest tell. Its five-year credit default swaps, the cost of insuring against the company defaulting, climbed to around 151 basis points in early October, levels last seen in 2009, according to market data cited by Bloomberg. S&P had already cut Oracle's credit rating to BBB-, a single notch above junk, back in July. The company is reportedly targeting more than $40 billion in additional debt and equity this fiscal year. That is on top of the $18 billion in bonds it sold in a single day last September, and the money is needed to keep funding its Texas, Wisconsin and New Mexico sites.

Demand for that paper has thinned out, too. Bonds from Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft and Oracle now trade at a premium to similarly rated non-AI corporate debt. Order books for their offerings have shrunk from roughly five times the amount on sale back in February to under two times by July, Bloomberg has reported. That is the difference between a bond that sells itself and one a bank has to work to place.

None of this is happening in isolation. The 10-year Treasury yield hit 5.304% this month, its highest since 2002, after a $39 billion auction cleared at 5.30%, the highest auction yield since 2000. The Federal Reserve's own September meeting minutes named AI-related corporate borrowing as a contributor to that move. Capital Economics argues the bigger driver is plain old inflation and government deficits, not tech company bond sales. Whoever is right about the cause, the effect is the same for anyone trying to finance a data center right now: the risk-free rate they are borrowing against just got a lot more expensive.

Frankly, the mechanics here matter more than the headline number. Banks do not sell down debt they are confident in. They sell down debt when they are worried about concentration, which is exactly what "approaching internal limits" means in plain English: too much of this bank's balance sheet is now one bet on one sector holding up. Spreading $120 billion of AI infrastructure spending across special purpose vehicles was supposed to make that risk easier to swallow. That is the structure Oracle, Meta, xAI and CoreWeave have all used to keep debt off their own balance sheets. Instead the risk is turning up at the banks that financed the SPVs in the first place.

The investors who still want in have gotten pickier about where. Capital is rotating toward data centers leased to investment-grade hyperscalers like Microsoft and Google, and away from weaker credits, Bloomberg has reported. That is exactly why CoreWeave-leased paper prices at 7.00% to 9.875%, against the 5.70% to 7.875% that hyperscaler-leased bonds command, per bond market data compiled by CCIR. A smaller, less capitalized AI infrastructure company trying to raise debt next quarter is now competing for the same nervous pool of lenders as Oracle. Except without Oracle's balance sheet or its existing customer base to point to.

That's the part of this story that does not show up in a single day's stock move. The AI boom still runs on the assumption that credit stays open indefinitely at reasonable terms. Six months of a bank struggling to sell $38 billion in loans is the clearest evidence yet that assumption is being tested in real time, not in some theoretical downturn still years away.
