item.title: Virtual Oxide Labs: Emulating a Full Oxide Rack (137 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://oxide.computer/blog/voxel-labs, See on Hacker News

The trouble with testing and developing for rack-scale hardware is that rack-scale is not all that easy to come by. I mean, nevermind the whole DDR5-as-a-currency thing; even if all the parts were available in abundance, any completed racks go swiftly to the front lines (AKA our customers' data centers).

As a member of the Product Assurance Team at Oxide, I find that totally unfair yet completely reasonable. And so we have to get a bit creative. We have to be able to:

  • Replicate diverse customer networking topologies

  • Run our actual control plane

  • Test up to date versions of our software

  • Represent the hardware components (we make racks, after all) including our switches and microcontrollers

And the cherry on top: we need to do that without cutting special "test version" releases. Because we want to keep our CI sleek, but also because that wouldn’t be playing fair.

Now, don’t get me wrong — we’re not without our tricks. When I joined Oxide last year, one of the first things I was introduced to was our racklettes; that is, smaller than average racks of four sleds and two switches each. These racklettes can be initialized and run just like a real rack, precisely because they are a real rack. Just not in any form factor it would be economical to sell. But for testing they work like a charm. We have four of them today, soon to be eight, where we can test any combination of hardware/software requirement.

We also have our various simulated methods of running Omicron. You can read more about those at How to Run Simulated and the full(er) How to Run Guide. I won’t go into a ton of detail here, but suffice it to say that most parts of our control plane (and more) can be run independently, in tandem, and in various degrees of simulation.

What’s a Voxel?

Do you remember the game Q*bert? It was one of the first wildly popular isometric games, and looked a little like this:

Why am I showing you a ridiculously small game screenshot? Well, each cube in that image represents a 'voxel,' or a point in 3D space. It’s actually the 3D version of a pixel. Volume Element + Pixel = Voxel. Neat, right?

Anyway, for Oxide, Virtual OXidE Labs (or Voxel) means an incredible amount of fidelity packed into a single piece of hardware. It is the spiritual successor to our prior virtual labs (known as a4x2) which allowed us to hack out decent racks running in VMs.

Pay attention to that word "fidelity" by the way. For it is, as Bryan Cantrill puts it, the Prime Directive: labs should use stock Oxide software without hack or modification.

This is what Voxel gives us. A complete software emulation stack, built on illumos in Rust, where we can build and test a variety of realistic configurations:

  • Sled virtualization provided by Propolis

  • BGP (numbered and unnumbered) or static networking with Debian and FRR

  • P4-powered switches via Oxide’s own SoftNPU, a software P4 switch

  • Microcontroller simulation and emulation for our Service Processor (SP) and Root of Trust (RoT)

And what’s more, it gives us all these features in a fairly small footprint. At home, I run Voxel labs on a Minisforum MS-A2 mini-PC with a 32-thread AMD Ryzen 9 9955HX and 96GB RAM. On that computer, I can spin up 6 sleds with ease, either in the form of one rack or in a multirack configuration (two separate racks, one management plane). All it requires is Oxide Helios and a decently fast NVMe drive. Launch, and in about 10 minutes you have a full Oxide rack with each "sled" in its own Propolis VM — alongside switches (also in Propolis) and other infrastructure.

Image Creation

Remember how I said we have to use stock Oxide software? That actually makes things easier. The first thing we do (following a common practice in hypervisor tooling) is to create a reusable snapshot.

Oxide sleds are only ever one of two things: a normal sled (a "gimlet" for the first generation, "cosmo" for the current) or a "scrimlet," which is a sled wired to the sidecar switches that runs a switch zone. It’s all amazingly elegant in its complexity, you should read more about it in our networking docs.

To create a snapshot for Voxel, all we must do is create a "sled" (virtual machine), install our control plane (Omicron) on it, snapshot it before the point of configuration, et voilà: a ready-to-launch sled. The control plane can be installed one of two ways:

From source

Voxel clones the Omicron repo on GitHub (or uses a locally defined source for rapid development) and uses cargo to compile

From TUF repo

We use Tufaceous to package Omicron releases using The Update Framework (TUF) and our CI tool Buildomat

Using the second option as an example, here’s the beginning of the process where voxel image create pulls out the key pieces that make up the sled config:

$ pfexec ./target/debug/voxel image create --from-tuf ../5d176e0be7e5cc0d3288c1bef10005ec31f2cd7c.zip 5d176e0be7e5cc0d3288c1bef10005ec31f2cd7c
[voxel] TUF source ../5d176e0be7e5cc0d3288c1bef10005ec31f2cd7c.zip: system version 23.0.0-0.ci+git5d176e0be7e, omicron 5d176e0be7e
[voxel] extracted 12 zones from ../5d176e0be7e5cc0d3288c1bef10005ec31f2cd7c.zip
[voxel] extracted 3 measurement corpus artifacts
[voxel] extracting host artifacts -> /export/home/helios/voxel-rawfix/target/debug/../../voxel-image/.tuf-host
[voxel] host boot image 1258295296 bytes, phase 1 rom 33554432 bytes
[voxel] extracted SP/RoT firmware -> /export/home/helios/voxel-rawfix/target/debug/../../voxel-image/.tuf-fw/ca9184058bd7

After a decent amount of unpacking and staging, it will launch a VM that everything gets written/installed to. And finally:

[voxel] ready: voxel-cp version=unknown unpacked_artifacts=18 built=2026-09-06T21:37:58
[voxel] clearing device-instance map, halting
[voxel] flushing, up to 25s
[voxel] stopping hypervisor
[voxel] writing voxel image voxel-cp-5d176e0be7e-tuf

That image is a zfs snapshot which can be used and reused to create our rack.

Ready for Launch

Launching the rack uses a similar process, except the control plane is already installed. All we need at this point is:

  1. An "frr" image (the Debian VMs for networking)

  2. A control plane image (like the one we just created)

  3. The voxel-init agent that gives each virtual sled its assignment

The log output is pretty long, but you can scroll through it if you’d like. I’ll recap after.

Like I said, a lot of steps. Here’s what happened:

  1. Trust material is generated in the form of sprockets PKI

  2. Emulated STM32H753 and LPC55 microcontrollers are flashed with Hubris firmware

  3. Our automated network topology suite (known as falcon) wires the topology with simnet and VNIC pairs for every link, and stages the sleds (g0, g1, and g2 in this case)

  4. Propolis VMs launch; 6 total in this example, with 3 driving the network and 3 as Oxide sleds

  5. voxel-init runs: a lightweight Rust agent on each node that

    • Sets up NAT and uplink addressing

    • Configures underlay setup on each sled

    • Writes the M.2 partition layout on emulated boot disks and labels five U.2 data disks

    • Seeds the host phase 2 image and install dataset to the M.2s

    • Assigns the scrimlets and runs a switch enforcer so they "remember" their identity across restarts

    • Activates sled-agent, the per-sled configuration layer for the control plane

  6. Connects to the commission API for wicketd, which brings the rack through its initialization phases

It’s a complex dance of steps, and I really buried the lede on the whole "emulated microcontrollers" front. But suffice it to say these are the complete and right steps for any Oxide rack, except the hardware is represented as distinct pieces of code. For example, need a new interconnect between two virtual racks? Add a couple lines of code in rack.rs.

There are a few things that don’t follow the Prime Directive (yet!). For example, those certs that make up the sprockets PKI up top aren’t set at manufacturing and coming from the RoT like our production racks. But that’s one of those things that we can live with for now, as it doesn’t affect actual rack runtime.

Emulating Service Processors

This is the bit I mentioned a moment ago. A big part of what makes our racks unique is the embedded RoT and SP in every sled. We’ve long had an SpSim construct that served as a stub for the service processor and would return the right info at the right times. But that’s simulation, not emulation. It’s always going to be happy path, and that’s just not enough fidelity for real testing cases.

As such, we built actual emulated Cortex-M7 and Cortex-M33 devices for illumos and Linux (x86 and ARM). The repo for this tool (sp-emu) is open source. Each of the two devices runs in a single thread, and (mostly) faithfully emulates the three main requirements: instructions, time, and interrupts.

From there, you can flash our Hubris firmware directly to these emulated devices, and then communicate by way of an ordinary socket. The Voxel lab can speak with these virtual devices via the Management Gateway Service (MGS) and Inter-Processor Communication Channel (IPCC). You can learn everything you want and more about these concepts in the Management Gateway Service repo and Hubris docs.

There really is no "run real microcontrollers as virtual devices with this one neat trick!" I can think of. But the real challenge of sp-emu’s job is time. Remember all of the code we’re running there is meant for silicon. Hubris schedules off a 1ms SysTick and the emulator doesn’t use wall time; as such, we had to invent a clock. That said, emulated hardware is also slower than the real thing. So there’s…​ well, less time per time. So instead of trying to get all temporal about it, time became instructions. For example, I give you maybe_tick:

if self.systick == 0 {
    self.systick = self.syst_rvr;
}
self.systick -= 1;
if self.systick == 0 {
    self.systick = self.syst_rvr;
    self.tick_events = self.tick_events.wrapping_add(1);
    if self.syst_csr & 2 != 0
        && self.mode == Mode::Thread
        && !self.primask
    {
        self.exception_entry(15, bus); // SysTick exception
    }
}

In this case, we count instructions against the kernel’s own reload value and fire exceptions anywhere the single-priority design makes it safe to take it — in thread mode, interrupts unmasked. By the same token, peripheral access costs one tick of our clock (an instruction), whereas on silicon it might stall for dozens of cycles on the bus.

You may have noticed self.exception_entry which is defined elsewhere in the code:

fn exception_entry(&mut self, vecnum: u32, bus: &mut Bus)

In short, this function models everything the hardware does on a Cortex-M core taking an exception, all the way between "exception becomes active" to the first handler instruction. vecnum here is an ARMv7-M exception number (also the vector table index for that exception’s handler). bus is the memory system which is used to actually push the frame and read the table.

Hubris has a non-preemptible kernel, though it schedules tasks preemptively. SVCall, PendSV, SysTick and all IRQs run at the same priority level, while faults keep a higher priority. As such, the emulator doesn’t have to nest handlers. It processes pending IRQs based on the PRIMASK, FAULTMASK, and BASEPRI settings. If one of them pended PendSV, that will perform the deferred context switch for the kernel. For more details on how it works internally, you can check this lovely bit of documentation.

if let Some(irq) = bus.next_irq() {
    if self.basepri == 0 || (bus.irq_prio(irq) as u32) < self.basepri {
        bus.clear_pending(irq);
        self.exception_entry(16 + irq as u32, bus);
        return;
    }
}
if bus.take_pendsv() {
    self.exception_entry(14, bus);
}

There’s a lot more we can talk about here, but to sum it all up you can look at this pseudo-ish loop:

loop {
    cpu.step(&mut bus, host.as_mut())?;   // one Thumb-2 instruction
    cpu.maybe_tick(&mut bus);             // SysTick: time is instructions
    cpu.maybe_interrupt(&mut bus);        // NVIC and PendSV delivery
    if cpu.cycles % 4096 == 0 {
        bus.pump_eth(host.as_mut());      // MGS packets in and out
        bus.pump_uart(host.as_mut());
    }
}

Note: yes I’m aware I said there’s no cycles then have a field named cycles. That’s the "fake it till you make it" part of emulation.

That’s the overall heartbeat of sp-emu, and it runs ad infinitum. Everything else exists to make those calls seem real.

And One More Thing

Past the actual working of the emulated sleds and microcontrollers, it’s all good ol' fashion user experience. When you’re running that many components on a single system, it can get really confusing trying to figure out what pieces are where, how to connect to one sled on one rack versus another, etc. So the voxel command that we use to launch and destroy virtual racks also serves as a connectivity tool. For example:

$ pfexec ./target/debug/voxel host login g0
[voxel] ssh root@192.168.68.167  (g0 global zone)
The illumos Project     helios-3.0.23976        May 2026
root@g0:~# zoneadm list
global
oxz_switch

That command logs the user straight into the g0 sled in the global zone. Alternatively:

$ pfexec ./target/debug/voxel tp login switch0
[voxel] ssh root@192.168.68.167 -> zlogin oxz_switch  (g0 switch0)

tp in this case acts like our technician ports, and allows the user to connect straight to a switch zone for rack-wide commands and networking. There are also numerous commands to manage things like images (export/import, delete), config (network topology, sled sizing, multi-rack, etc.), and more features coming as we build.

Voxel is available under the MPL 2.0 license for download. You’ll need to run Helios as your OS to run Voxel. I’d recommend 16+ threads and 64GB+ RAM, plus a good premium NVMe with onboard DRAM.

item.title: America didn't lose its rare earth industry, it sold it (184 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.lawfaremedia.org/article/america-didn-t-lose-its-rare-earth-industry.-it-sold-it, See on Hacker News

In October 2025, Beijing imposed sweeping controls on its rare earth exports. Since then, those controls have been suspended one short reprieve at a time, in the latest instance until Nov. 10, with a broader trade truce through Jan. 10, 2027. The reprieves have repeatedly come only after American concessions, demonstrating China’s leverage in the export fight.

Yet China has constricted sales even during the truce, as buyers have few options but to take what they can get. In June, with the suspension in force, Beijing placed MP Materials and USA Rare Earth, the two companies the U.S. is counting on to build an alternative supply to China, on an export control list.

Washington’s effort to rebuild the supply chain, meanwhile, has not yet reached the scale or durability the problem requires. With up to $100 billion in loan authority specifically earmarked for critical minerals in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, the capital undoubtedly exists. What is missing is alignment of interests among the parties that would supply and benefit from it, and a political system patient enough to hold a course for the decade or more that rebuilding a supply chain takes.

This article’s authors work at the intersection of finance and national security. Between the three of us, we have watched the same on-again, off-again rhythm play out in both Chinese statecraft and U.S. budget fights. A consistent pattern plays out: Capital markets are good at financing efficient supply but are not good at financing a binary outcome, such as insurance against a monopoly state seller that can manipulate both price and availability. And subsidies alone will not close that gap. We have seen firsthand that what the U.S. government has to offer right now insufficiently incentivizes private investors, because its tools are market tools deployed in an environment of market failure. Instead, we propose a financing instrument that could clear both economic and political hurdles: a contingent convertible security that converts into ownership if Beijing weaponizes supply.

Rare Earths Are a Market Failure

The history of how we got here is well known, but worth retelling briefly. The Chinese Communist Party inherited its strategic focus on building industrial capacity from the Soviet Union. In 1964, Deng Xiaoping inspected an iron ore mine near the Mongolian border holding the world’s largest rare earth deposit. He ordered the engineers to develop steel and rare earths alike. Since then, as technologies have increasingly relied on specialized materials, the Chinese Communist Party under successive leaders has deliberately invested in and consolidated control over the rare earths industry. China refines more than 90 percent of the world’s rare earths and close to 99 percent of heavy rare earths today. It processes nearly all the heavy elements that go into precision-guided weapons and advanced chips.

When Beijing tightened export controls in October 2025, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent characterized it as “pointing a bazooka at the supply chains and industrial base of the entire free world.” Remarkably, the entire market for rare earth oxides is worth less than $10 billion. That a $10 billion market can grind to a halt trillions in global gross domestic product is the definition of a chokepoint. Beijing controls this chokepoint today by design. Decades of state policy work laid the groundwork for the Chinese Communist Party to enact an international licensing system by 2025. General Secretary Xi Jinping himself openly speaks about the importance of maintaining global dependency on China’s industrial supply chains.

Hindsight treats this as neglect, something policymakers lost sight of and let slip during the U.S.’s unipolar moment. That is a necessary, but only partial, explanation. The truth is the United States did not lose its rare earth industry due to carelessness. Private American companies willingly sold it, for reasons that made perfect economic sense at the time and still do. China bought it for reasons that were never purely economic. That mismatch explains why, after years of investment and policy attention, the dependency remains.

Until the late 1980s, the United States was the world’s leading producer and refiner of rare earths. But it was a dirty business: The Mountain Pass mine in California leaked roughly 600,000 gallons of radioactive and other waste into the Mojave. As cleanup and regulatory costs mounted and profits fell, the mine shut down in stages starting in the 1990s until it was fully idle by 2002. Meanwhile, the work moved to China, where the state subsidized unprofitable operations, tolerated pollution, and sold the processed oxides back to the U.S. at rock-bottom prices.

The same thing happened to the magnets: In 1995, General Motors sold Magnequench, its magnet unit, to a Chinese-backed consortium. By 2006, the last U.S. plant had closed, and the machine tools and equipment had been shipped to China. Economists would say this was the right move for a free market economy. Comparative advantage did what it was supposed to do, and a dirty, low-margin business left a wealthy country for a developing one. There was even a strategic rationale: Drawing China into the trading system, the wishful thinking went, would also make it a responsible stakeholder rather than a rival.

The category error was to conceive rare earths as a market, rather than recognizing it as a geostrategic industry. A market solves for the lowest cost. To be sure, Chinese producers competed on cost, and they rode a tech boom with surging demand for their product. But a state will pay almost any price to control a chokepoint, because tolerating a money-losing business pales in comparison to the geopolitical leverage that it brings. Over time, China has become less market driven, not more. Meanwhile, the U.S. continued to treat as a market what the Chinese Communist Party came to appreciate as a strategic program.

Control over the chokepoint gives Beijing a switch. When it lets the material flow, no private interest will build alternative supply chains at scale, because Chinese state-funded producers can sell at or below cost indefinitely, and no rational private investor will willingly sign up to lose money. When China cuts off the flow, the incentives reverse overnight, but capacity cannot follow overnight, because standing up the full supply chain and rebuilding the lost know-how can take a decade or longer.

This is classic market failure in which the same critical material can become worthless or priceless on command. In 2010, during a maritime dispute with Japan, Beijing reportedly halted rare earth shipments, and Tokyo quickly conceded. The short-term truces of the past year, each struck around contentious but episodic trade disputes, further entrench that market failure. Each successive loosening and tightening seems designed to keep the United States and its allies off balance and frustrate any long-term plan to reduce Beijing’s leverage.

Government Money Has to Survive Politics

If the market will not rebuild the rare earths supply chain, the government must do so.

Administrations under both parties have tried, and their attempts have run into a predictable morass of misaligned interests. The parties to government financing all want different things. Private investors want attractive returns in fat years, while having the government carry losses in lean ones. Commercial lenders want years of fully contracted offtake to guarantee interest payments, while Congress typically appropriates money for the next year. Markets want flexibility while Congress wants tight oversight and guardrails. Washington often wants to be the last (and lightest) money in, which signals to investors that the government is hedging. And cheap, open-ended financing is exactly the wrong signal to send to management teams.

The Pentagon’s latest playbook acknowledges that the market, left to its own devices, simply will not finance uneconomic redundancy. As a result, the July 2025 deal with MP Materials includes $400 million in convertible preferred stock, loans, equity warrants, a 10-year guaranteed price floor, and a 10-year offtake commitment. The deal was right for its moment, as it gets the producer going and sustains it while Beijing floods the market. But the deal blurs two different roles: In ordinary years, the government is a lender, financing capacity the market will not; in a crisis, it has insured against a geopolitical event. These two roles call for two different return profiles. Because the deal does not separate them, it puts the government in the unenviable position of simultaneously absorbing losses and inviting the charge of nationalization, all without a clear exit strategy.

Without some structure to navigate potentially painful political costs, these financing arrangements will come under pressure during budget cycles and electoral turnover. And that is simply untenable, because when it comes to the decade-plus timeline to stand up a rare earths supply chain, whatever Washington builds must outlast the administration that built it.

A Financial Instrument That Responds to Beijing’s Behavior

Our proposal is a financial instrument that aligns these interests. In financial parlance, the instrument is called a contingent convertible security, also known as a CoCo bond, issued by the producer to the government and any private lenders who wish to join, paired with guaranteed offtake at a price floor. Its form changes with two externally observable conditions: the producer’s capacity build-out and Beijing’s behavior.

Here’s how it works. In its starting form (and in quiet years), a CoCo bond is a simple loan paying interest. Two triggers change its form. The first is capacity. The producer must cross a defined capacity threshold by a fixed date. Capacity can be measured as units of output in mining, refining, or manufacturing critical minerals. Management’s immediate incentives should be tied to the build-out itself.

The second trigger is either a sustained breach of an agreed price band or an externally observed exercise of the chokepoint. This could be denial of export licenses, a bureaucratic delay beyond a specified period, or another form of “constructive denial” that materially interrupts supply to the United States or allied countries. Importantly, no part of this trigger should rely on Beijing’s confirmation, because it is not incentivized to admit to a cutoff. The trigger should be narrow enough that it cannot be declared for political convenience, but broad enough that an adversary cannot game it simply by changing the form of the restriction.

When the first trigger fires, the lender receives a pro rata share of the producer’s free cash flow, in effect, a dividend. The lender paid to build the capacity, so it shares in what that capacity earns. When both triggers fire, the lender also gains the right to convert into common equity. The conversion event does not create new capacity—the financing has already done that work—but rather matches the payoff to the risk. If lenders financed years of otherwise uneconomic capacity because a cutoff might someday make it necessary, they share in the upside if and when the cutoff comes. The cash participation matters too: In a crisis, the market may treat a price spike as temporary and event-driven and not value the equity, but the spike still flows through the producer’s cash flow, which benefits the lender either way.

Why would a producer agree to this? Because it gets something unique that the market will not otherwise provide. In effect, the producer buys a put—the price floor that carries it through Beijing’s dumping—and pays for it by selling a call—the cash share and the conversion right. It trades some of the windfall in a crisis for the protection of surviving quiet years. Either way, the taxpayer is paid for the risk actually borne, when it is borne, rather than for a risk merely feared.

Nor does the government have to finance the entire CoCo bond. Pre-vetted private co-investors, including foreign co-investors subject to Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States (CFIUS) screening, can offset government money dollar-for-dollar. Ideally, co-investors should be firms that fear a cutoff the most, such as defense contractors and automakers. Private co-investors would receive a pro rata right to offtake as a further incentive and could potentially even trade the bond with its associated offtake rights with other investors. Japan’s JARE consortium did something similar when it financed Australia’s Lynas in return for supply. Finally, private holders also give the program a constituency that outlasts any single administration.

Neither Nationalization nor Welfare

This instrument compensates for the asymmetric risk a lender (whether taxpayer or private) assumes when countering an adversary-controlled chokepoint, by providing an asymmetric reward if that chokepoint is ever exercised.

The risk here is not from a natural shortage or an ordinary price cycle, but from the Chinese Communist Party’s policy decisions. The same logic reaches other chokepoint materials such as pharmaceutical precursors. Rare earths are the clearest case and, at under $10 billion in market size, the cheapest place for the U.S. government to start. And it can start under existing authorities. For example, the Pentagon has leaned on Title III of the Defense Production Act for its recent mineral deals involving equity. The Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital can lend, but its equity authority remains unclear. The Senate is currently revising the National Defense Authorization Act for 2027 to clarify those authorities. Its language should cover instruments like this CoCo bond.

Our CoCo bond proposal does not replace stockpiles, price floors, or offtake agreements. These instruments solve significant but different problems. Stockpiles buy time in a crisis, price floors protect producers against predatory pricing, and offtake agreements guarantee demand. The CoCo bond, in contrast, distributes risk and reward to investors in a binary, geopolitical event outside the producer’s control. It also enables the government to lend as a portfolio—some developers will fail, but the winners, and any crisis, can carry the portfolio as a whole. And it may have some deterrent effect as well: If this instrument makes capacity more likely to get built, and that prospect enters Beijing’s risk calculus, so much the better.

Economically, the conversion right works like the equity warrants the Pentagon took in MP Materials. The difference lies in the quiet years, when under this structure the government holds no equity. Outright equity stakes invite the charge of nationalization; cheap financing with no upside smacks of corporate welfare. We believe a structure that is intentionally designed to avoid both at the outset—but flexible enough to change form in response to an adversary’s actions, not domestic political developments—has the best chance of surviving enough political cycles to complete a decade-plus build-out.

*          *          *

Translating this concept into reality raises important implementation questions about statutory authority, precise trigger definitions, CFIUS integration, and corporate governance. We offer the CoCo bond model to stimulate discussions around aligning interests in a market failure and national security context, and we invite the legal, policy, and financial communities to help refine the “plumbing” necessary to make asymmetric financing a workable pillar of U.S. statecraft.

A market will always sell a chokepoint to whoever runs it cheapest, and by market logic, it would be the right thing to do. Subsidies alone cannot win it back, because they only affect price; Beijing prices for geopolitical leverage, not profit. Neutralizing a chokepoint created through market failure requires capital willing to absorb years of subpar returns or even losses against an extraordinary geopolitical crisis. In quiet years, the government should earn like a lender, with the price floor protecting against Beijing’s dumping. When capacity is built, it should share in what it financed. And if Beijing ever reaches for the switch, the taxpayers and private investors who paid to insure against that moment should participate in the value their capital created. The risk is asymmetric. The financing should be too.

item.title: AI agents aren't 'going rogue.' Frontier labs are skipping security basics (926 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.csoonline.com/article/4234854/ai-agents-arent-going-rogue-frontier-labs-are-skipping-security-basics.html, See on Hacker News

Cyber experts say AI labs’ containment and monitoring failures — not agents with minds of their own — are to blame for recent alarming hacking reports. CISOs should vet their AI vendors and tighten security basics as safeguards.

Since July, US frontier AI labs and other AI leaders have revealed a string of incidents in which their models accessed external computer systems without authorization, events popularly described as AI agents “going rogue.”

The most well-known and studied of these incidents is OpenAI’s hack into Hugging Face, which OpenAI initially characterized as “an unprecedented cyber incident, involving state-of-the-art cyber capabilities,” and later said was due to “misaligned behavior,” or behavior its creators did not intend.

Following news of the Hugging Face incident, Anthropic revealed that one of its models gained unauthorized access to the production infrastructure of three organizations; Meta said one of its AI models hacked another company ​during cybersecurity testing; and Google confessed that its Gemini model carried out three “undirected computer hacks.”

Although press reports and the model providers themselves use language such as rogue agents or misalignment, cybersecurity experts who spoke with CSO argue that language obscures a simple truth: These incidents were caused by inexcusable failures by the frontier labs to implement cybersecurity practices that have been well-known for decades.

Compounding the problem, according to a half dozen cybersecurity experts CSO interviewed at three industry conferences in September and in subsequent conversations, is that the frontier labs, particularly OpenAI and Anthropic, have rejected their advice on how to improve their cybersecurity risk management practices to avoid these kinds of surreptitious hacks, often lumping cybersecurity practices under “AI safety,” in which they believe they have superior expertise.

“They are not as good as they think they are, honestly,” Gary McGraw, co-founder of the Berryville Institute of Machine Learning, tells CSO. “It would be better if they had more respect for expertise that is hard-earned from people in all sorts of subsets of security, like forensics or security engineering, building sandboxes, setting up or monitoring network security situations.”

Neither Anthropic nor OpenAI responded to CSO’s requests for comment.

Inexcusable failures on cybersecurity basics, particularly containment

According to the cybersecurity professionals CSO spoke with, one of the biggest cybersecurity failures by the frontier AI labs is the lack of implementation of tried-and-true containment practices that stretch back to the 1990s, such as setting up secure sandboxes that would effectively bar agents from escaping their test environments.

“These are things that we’ve been dealing with for years,” Rob T. Lee, chief AI officer and chief of research at SANS Institute, tells CSO. “There’s no reason why every single time this happens, it’s, ‘Oops, we don’t know how they got out.’”

“You can tell that their security teams are fairly nascent,” Lee says. “Folks on the cybersecurity containment side do argue that the majority of reasons that we’re seeing containment breached is that it’s not set up correctly.”

Lee adds, “The Hugging Face incident definitively showed that it wasn’t the fact that the agents were super smart. It’s that there literally was a hole that was exploited because it was not configured correctly on the containment side.”

Dan Wallach, expert technical resident at RAND’s Center on AI, Security, and Technology, thinks the security failures of the AI labs boil down to the fact that they don’t prioritize cybersecurity.

“I would say they are not prioritizing cybersecurity,” he tells CSO. “I don’t think I can say that for all of the labs,” Wallach says, pointing to French AI lab Mistral’s launch of its Large 4 AI model, which the company said tried to operate beyond its testing environment before Mistral cut it off.

And, he adds, “It’s not rocket science to isolate one of these AI things. Security people have been talking about how to do either air-gapping, so there’s literally no electrical way for data to get from here to here, or absent that, to have really strong egress control to make sure that nothing pushes through.”

On top of that, the frontier labs appear to be conducting insufficient monitoring of their agents’ behavior. The Hugging Face incident “went on for days, and nobody noticed,” Wallach says. “People started these experiments and weren’t watching them. That’s an absence of control. And then they’re surprised by what happened.”

Divorcing safety from security

One barrier to persuading frontier labs to up their security game is the intense focus they have on what they call “safety,” which they don’t extend to traditional cybersecurity practices.

“I can see how security behavior looks like AI safety,” RAND’s Wallach says. “But if the way that you’re evaluating this AI tool is by unleashing it on the internet and seeing what happens, then this is what classical security tooling is for.”

SANS Institute’s Lee says, “If these frontier labs really wanted to test their stuff, they need to beef up their cybersecurity component. But their gut reaction in the response to their agents getting out is to say, ‘It’s not a cybersecurity problem.’ It has literally become an AI safety problem, which is divorced from the cybersecurity side.”

Many AI experts suggest that if the AI companies were to embrace advice from cybersecurity specialists, it could help put an end to the kind of unrestrained AI agent behavior causing concerns. “AI safety focuses on the rules of the road,” Lee says. “Everything is about guardrail rules.”

But “I do believe cybersecurity can contain AI,” he says. “We just need to be in the room where it happens and have a seat at the table. It’s important for our field to be as close to the AI safety folks as possible.”

Bad cybersecurity could increase liability

If frontier labs are overlooking cybersecurity fundamentals that could reduce or eliminate the types of incidents that have created widespread concerns, that strengthens the case that they should be held liable for their “rogue” agents. The insurance industry is already lining up on the side of holding AI industry executives liable for these actions.

Democratic Senators have introduced legislation that would hold AI agent operators liable for hacking incidents. Even the AI-friendly White House has seemingly concluded that the companies should be held liable for their errant agents, while the US Federal Trade Commission is conducting a probe into Anthropic, OpenAI, and other AI labs into the dangers their technologies pose to consumers.

However, in recent legislative and council hearings, lab representatives have held fast to the notion that they are not responsible for AI agents run amok.

Experts say this position is untenable, particularly in light of the labs’ cybersecurity failures.

BIML’s McGraw characterizes the labs’ position as: “Don’t send the lawyers to us, send it to our program. It’s our program’s fault.” His assessment of that argument: “That’s just high BS.”

He also questions whether the labs’ operational failures undermine confidence in their broader security capabilities. “They live inside their own bubble,” he says. “The fact that they cannot do clear, easy operations properly does not bode well for their capabilities in security engineering, which is much harder to do.”

SANS Lee says, “That’s where the traceability for both liability and insurance comes into play, because if one of these agents is detected, and they’re able to trace it back to the person that initiated it, liability’s going to kick in and say, ‘Hey, you, you broke the law, ergo, we need to prosecute.’”

What security leaders should do now

Even as evidence mounts that frontier labs are not implementing sound cybersecurity practices, and the debate over liability remains unsolved, CISOs and other security leaders can take steps to protect themselves from AI model misfires.

First, when it comes to assessing tools based on frontier lab models, “I would always get an external entity to help with that,” McGraw says. “AI is extremely powerful and extremely useful, but it comes with very serious grown-up risks that do impact the enterprise. Identify those risks, put in the right controls, make sure that AI adoption is not just arbitrary and willy-nilly and all over the enterprise, but has some centralized authority that is looking at the problem, and then get ready for the next big thing, which is swarms of agents.”

For Lee, the best protection is to ask the right questions. “It starts with asking the right questions and then finding the tools and capabilities for those [AI labs] that are able to demonstrate a higher level of cybersecurity competency,” he says. “You’re really looking for the people on the teams that are dealing with really hard problems.”

But fundamentally, the best preparation to deal with AI model cyber weaknesses is to make sure all the long-standing cybersecurity risk management practices are in place across the organization. “This is the least exciting part of the discussion,” Wallach says. “It’s the cyber version of ‘eat your vegetables.’”

“We need to re-engineer our software so it has better security,” he adds. “We need to have multi-factor authentication on all of our accounts. We need to eat our vegetables from a defensive cyber perspective. And we know how to do it.”

At the recently concluded Maintainers Summit, Linus Torvalds said that he had been using a large language model to work on a patch series addressing a longstanding problem; he has now posted that series for review.
The fairly short series of ten patches basically enhances folio lookup by noticing when folios are hot, and setting a "delay releasing this folio until after a RCU period", and then using that RCU delay it does not just the folio lookup itself under RCU (which we've done forever), but also the actual folio data accesses themselves under RCU. item.title: Better HTTP/1 connection reuse in Go 1.27 (224 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://go.dev/blog/http-connection-reuse, See on Hacker News

Take a look at the following function:

func getStatus(url string) (int, error) {
    resp, err := http.Get(url)
    if err != nil {
        return 0, err
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    return resp.StatusCode, nil
}

It sends a GET request to url and returns the HTTP status code.

Using HTTP/1 (GODEBUG=http2client=0), calling this function 100 times against index.golang.org takes ~710 milliseconds on Go 1.26 on my machine. On Go 1.27, the same program takes ~150 milliseconds.

That is almost 5 times faster! How is such a drastic performance difference possible?

The cost of establishing HTTP connections

To understand the difference, consider what happens on the network when we make an HTTP request.

Go’s net/http package supports HTTP/1.0, HTTP/1.1, and HTTP/2. All three run over TCP, and usually over TLS when talking to HTTPS endpoints. Making a request over a new connection looks something like this:

  1. TCP handshake (1 RTT): the client sends a SYN packet, the server replies with SYN-ACK, and the client replies with ACK. Because the client can send the first TLS message alongside that final ACK, establishing the TCP connection takes 1 round-trip time (RTT).
  2. TLS handshake (2 RTT): next, a TLS handshake exchanges encryption keys and verifies the server’s identity; using TLS 1.2, this takes 2 RTT.
  3. HTTP request: with the keys exchanged, HTTP requests can finally be sent after a total of 3 RTT.

These round trips (plus some CPU time spent on TLS handshakes) add up quickly. In cross-region communications, one-way latencies often reach or exceed the 50 ms (100 ms RTT) shown in the diagram above. Compared to the 300 ms spent just setting up the connection, the HTTP request itself can be cheap to serve, taking only a little over 1 RTT when bandwidth is plentiful or the HTTP response is small.

Even in more favorable conditions, opening a new connection can still be expensive. Our opening benchmark queries index.golang.org, which is distributed worldwide and supports TLS 1.3. This means that latency is relatively low, and the TLS handshake can actually finish in just 1 RTT. Even so, the performance difference is still very noticeable.

Connection reuse

To avoid paying this setup cost on every request, HTTP clients and servers try to reuse existing connections across multiple requests when possible. The mechanics of this differ based on the HTTP version:

  • HTTP/1.0: while not part of the official specification, clients and servers often opt into connection reuse by sending a Connection: keep-alive header. Reuse continues until either endpoint omits the header or sends a Connection: close header.
  • HTTP/1.1: connections are persistent by default, and can be reused for subsequent requests and responses unless either side declares otherwise by sending a Connection: close header.
  • HTTP/2: multiple requests and responses can be multiplexed over a single TCP connection.

When connection reuse fails

In HTTP/1 (both HTTP/1.0 and HTTP/1.1), multiple requests and responses on the same connection are sent sequentially on the wire. If two GET requests are sent to index.golang.org over the same TCP connection, the responses arrive as a single stream of bytes:

As shown in the diagram, net/http.Get reads and parses the status line and headers from the byte stream to populate net/http.Response, then returns immediately. The response body remains unread on the connection and is consumed only as the caller reads from net/http.Response.Body.

Because responses are sent back-to-back on the same stream, net/http can only find the start of the next response after the current response body has been read to the very end (as determined by the Content-Length or Transfer-Encoding header).

Now look back at our example program, where we never read resp.Body:

func getStatus(url string) (int, error) {
    resp, err := http.Get(url)
    if err != nil {
        return 0, err
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    return resp.StatusCode, nil
}

Through Go 1.26, when resp.Body.Close is called, net/http sees that there is still an unread response body. Realizing that it cannot reuse the connection, it abandons the existing connection and creates new connections for its next requests, causing it to repeatedly incur the cost of establishing new connections.

(HTTP/2 does not have this problem. Because it multiplexes streams of frames over a single connection rather than sending responses strictly back-to-back, an unread response body on one stream does not block other requests from sharing the connection.)

Where failed connection reuse hurts

This subtlety of HTTP/1 connection reuse can cause silent performance degradation in seemingly innocuous code.

As in our opening example, a client might only care about an API response’s status code. However, the API endpoint it is talking to might send bodies that provide more detailed but ultimately unused information, such as {"success": true, "message": "update processed"}. This will unfortunately cause connection reuse to fail.

Even programs that do read the response body can run into this issue if they stop just short of the end of the body. For example, encoding/json.Decoder stops reading as soon as it sees the closing } of a JSON object. If a server sends a JSON response terminated with a newline, decoding the JSON object will leave the newline still unread. The connection cannot be reused for a new request until that newline is consumed. Thus, a healthy connection might end up being abandoned, even though it was only a single byte away from being reusable.

The manual solution

The unread body problem has been a long-standing sharp edge. Over the years, many Go developers came up with their own workarounds. Most commonly, this is done by draining the response body prior to closing it:

func getStatus(url string) (int, error) {
    resp, err := http.Get(url)
    if err != nil {
        return 0, err
    }
    drainAndCloseBody(resp.Body)
    return resp.StatusCode, nil
}

func drainAndCloseBody(body io.ReadCloser) {
    io.Copy(io.Discard, body) // Drain the response body before closing it.
    body.Close()
}

While this works for small responses, if the unread body is large, establishing a new TCP connection can be faster than downloading and discarding the rest of the body. A better approach is to cap the number of bytes we are willing to drain:

func drainAndCloseBody(body io.ReadCloser) {
    io.CopyN(io.Discard, body, 256<<10) // Only drain up to 256 KB.
    body.Close()
}

However, a server might send a response body that trickles in slowly, so we also need to cap the time we spend draining:

func drainAndCloseBody(body io.ReadCloser) {
    drainDone := make(chan struct{}, 1)
    go func() {
        io.CopyN(io.Discard, body, 256<<10) // Only drain up to 256 KB.
        drainDone <- struct{}{}
    }()
    // Only spend at most 50 ms trying to drain the response body.
    select {
    case <-drainDone:
    case <-time.After(50 * time.Millisecond):
        // If we reach the 50 ms timeout, body.Close will run and interrupt the
        // io.CopyN, preventing goroutine leaks.
    }
    body.Close()
}

Of course, we also do not want to block for up to 50 milliseconds when closing a response body. Instead, we can drain the body asynchronously in the background and let it race against subsequent requests:

func drainAndCloseBody(body io.ReadCloser) {
    drainDone := make(chan struct{}, 1)
    go func() {
        io.CopyN(io.Discard, body, 256<<10) // Only drain up to 256 KB.
        drainDone <- struct{}{}
    }()
    go func() {
        // Only spend at most 50 ms trying to drain the response body.
        select {
        case <-drainDone:
            // If the drain can finish before a new request is sent, the
            // connection will be reused; otherwise, a new connection is
            // created, and the current connection will be put in a pool of
            // idle connections, potentially being reused for another future
            // request.
        case <-time.After(50 * time.Millisecond):
            // If we reach the 50 ms timeout, body.Close will run and interrupt
            // the io.CopyN, preventing goroutine leaks.
        }
        body.Close()
    }()
}

As we can see, draining response bodies safely is surprisingly tricky and cumbersome. Worse, as the practice of draining response bodies spread, some nuances were often lost. This has led to misunderstandings such as attempting to drain response bodies for HTTP/2 connections, when doing so is unnecessary.

The current state and conclusion

Starting in Go 1.27, net/http.Transport automatically does everything we have implemented in the code above: it will asynchronously drain an unread HTTP/1 response body for up to 50 ms or 256 KB. It also implements additional optimizations; for example, when a response contains the Connection: close header, draining the body is guaranteed to be wasted work, and it therefore skips doing so. Note that this behavior might evolve in future versions of Go, as other possible enhancements become apparent.

As a general best practice, we now recommend that users simply close their HTTP bodies once they no longer need them, like in our original example:

func getStatus(url string) (int, error) {
    resp, err := http.Get(url)
    if err != nil {
        return 0, err
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    return resp.StatusCode, nil
}

Go is all about simplicity. Let your code stay clean and simple, and let net/http deal with the complexities on your behalf.

item.title: ICE Planning $100M 'Nightmare' Domestic Spy Program (496 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://prospect.org/2026/10/14/ice-planning-nightmare-domestic-spy-program-ero-one/, See on Hacker News

Immigration and Customs Enforcement is fast-tracking a $100 million domestic surveillance program to put 142 intelligence agents in more than two dozen cities and the District of Columbia, in what contracting and surveillance experts said would be a significant expansion of the agency’s ability to reach into private lives.

The new program is called the Enforcement and Removal Operations Overwatch and National Security Enforcement, or ERO ONE, described in documents posted last month on federal procurement websites.

More from Whitney Curry Wimbish

Under the program, agents would analyze classified and unclassified information to identify “trends, patterns, relationships, threats, and intelligence gaps,” and provide ICE with briefings for Enforcement and Removal Operation missions, according to a statement of work published on September 18. A forecasting document published a week earlier said that the solicitation will likely be released on December 10. Intelligence contracting experts said the timeline suggests ICE will award the contract around February.

“It looks dangerously like the construction of an internal spying agency,” said Jay Stanley, senior policy analyst with the American Civil Liberties Union’s Speech, Privacy, and Technology Project, who has written extensively on immigration agencies’ mass surveillance. “It’s a nightmare in the making.”

It’s also a weapon that the government will likely use against not only undocumented immigrants, but everyone else, too. That includes political enemies, intelligence experts said. Speaking with the Prospect on Monday as news broke that the Trump regime had raided progressive Minnesota Rep. Ilhan Omar’s D.C. home, former military intelligence analyst Michael Wriston said that “you’d expect to see more of this” under ERO ONE.

“Not just necessarily sitting members of Congress, but anyone, and especially members of the immigrant community,” Wriston said. “No one is safe. No one.”

THE PLAN DOES NOT SPECIFY WHAT OR WHOM ICE is looking for with this increased spying capability. But one of the components that caused former intelligence contractors’ concern was that ERO ONE agents will analyze both classified and nonclassified information to produce “network, link and relationship” analyses. That type of analysis involves researching not only a target, but also every other person to whom they’re connected, including household members, family members, friends, acquaintances, or the person with whom they carpool to work.

According to the statement of work, contractors will be tasked with conducting analytical research “to identify and assess relationships among individuals, organizations, locations, events, activities, data points, and other entities.” They will review information to identify “known, reported, or potential relationships; recurring patterns; organizational structures; associations; areas of convergence; temporal or geographic connections; and other linkages relevant to the assigned intelligence requirement.” Contractors will then “evaluate the significance and reliability” of the relationships and “prepare link charts, network diagrams, timelines, analytical summaries, written assessments, or other related products” for ICE to use.

Military intelligence agents compile the same type of research, Wriston said. He knows because he did that job.

The Prospect in your inbox

Analysis that goes beyond the noise with in-depth, progressive reporting.

No paywall, no programmatic ads — just the reporting. Unsubscribe anytime. Submitting your email signs you up for The Daily Prospect, our weekday morning newsletter.

“We’ve seen this time and time again. It’s the imperial boomerang,” said Wriston, who is also a data journalist and the founder of ICE watchdog group Project Salt Box, where he reported on ERO ONE the day the first document went live and has written about it since. “These are the kinds of things that happened in Afghanistan, Iraq, Yemen, Syria, for years. Now that methodology is being brought into the ICE space.”

Federal documents likewise do not detail the specific sources of information agents will analyze, only that all agents must possess previously awarded active top secret clearance, with eligibility to access Sensitive Compartmented Information. That’s a type of information that must be accessed through certain formal control systems managed by the Director of National Intelligence, a position held by Trump ally Jay Clayton. The agents will not make any decisions about what to do with the information they compile.

Wriston said that except for the fact that ICE officials are trying to make immigration a matter of national security, it’s unclear why they need this program when they already have the Homeland Security Investigations unit, which conducted the raid on Omar’s house, to research targets. His immediate worry, he said, is that the program will make it easier for the government to find terrified immigrants hiding at home because they think they’ll be safe there.

ICE PLANS TO SEND THE 142 AGENTS, plus two project managers, to locations in Atlanta, Boston, Buffalo, Chicago, Dallas, D.C., Denver, Detroit, El Paso, Harlingen (Texas), Houston, Laguna Niguel (California), Los Angeles, Miami, New Orleans, New York, Newark, Philadelphia, Phoenix, Salt Lake City, San Antonio, San Diego, San Francisco, Seattle, St. Paul, and Williston (Vermont), according to the statement of work.

Details in the document, and the rapid timeline, show that the Trump administration intends to use the program immediately, said Brian Murphy, a government contractor who worked for 25 years with ICE parent agency DHS. It’s rare for the government to only want workers with top secret clearance, he said.

“I’ve only seen it when there is an imminent need to work on something right now,” he told the Prospect. “Trump has two years in office. He can’t wait … they want to get rolling on this immediately.”

The program description is so broad that Murphy said he thinks the goal goes beyond targeting immigrants. “I think it’s darker than that,” because the agency could use the intelligence to attack people with identities and views the Trump regime doesn’t like. “The question for DHS is, what is the threat they’re trying to go after?”

The federal government can easily change who qualifies as a threat and produce data that backs up the reasoning, Murphy said, and used as an example annual Homeland Threat Assessments. In 2020, Secretary of Homeland Security Chad Wolf identified white supremacist extremists as “the most persistent and lethal threat in the Homeland.” But by last year, that threat had disappeared from the report, except to appear once in a glossary of terms. The rest of the report focused heavily on Trump administration priorities as national security threats, including immigrants crossing the border with Mexico and transnational criminal organizations.

In addition, the murders of Renee Good and Alex Pretti have shown how the government views protesters against ICE abductions as an abiding threat. In a national security directive known as NSPM-7, President Trump identified anti-fascist protesters as domestic terrorists and proposed an architecture to disrupt and counter dissent.

“If you want to draw a narrative that the real threat to America is whatever you want it to be, you can very easily do that. You just stop gathering intel on militias,” Murphy said. “It’s like any other police state. If you ask it to find something to make my opponents the enemy, well, you can do that.”

Legal liability should be a major concern for anyone who bids on the ERO ONE contract, Murphy said, because it’s unclear whether the information they’d be charged with accessing had been gathered legally. He added, “It’s very, very concerning that they’re fast-tracking this.”

Stanley, the ACLU analyst, noted that immigration officials across agencies have been using an excessive amount of surveillance tools for years, including their “Stingray” cell tower simulators, automatic license plate readers, and tools that track location from cellphones. They use a facial recognition and biometric collection app called Mobile Fortify, a Palantir app called ImmigrationOS to track immigrants’ movements, and buy data from LexisNexis to identify someone’s family and work history. ERO ONE would draw on all of that information, plus an expanded group of sources to reach into the private lives of anyone it wants, intelligence experts said.

ICE already knows its potential bidders for ERO ONE, said Diana Brozi, the procurement specialist listed on the document. She told the Prospect it was unlikely the agency would hold an industry day and declined to provide further information.

DHS did not respond to a request for information or comment on the claim that the program could be used to spy on political enemies.

Een eenheid van de Amsterdamse politie heeft dinsdag bij een datacenter op het Science Park in Amsterdam een server in beslag genomen van de Italiaanse internetdienstverlener Autistici/Inventati (A/I). Dat is gebeurd op basis van een Amerikaans rechtshulpverzoek. Een kopie van de inhoud van de server wordt nu naar de VS gestuurd.

A/I was een linkse antikapitalistische organisatie die de afgelopen vijfentwintig jaar gratis webhosting en e-maildiensten aanbood aan zo’n twintigduizend organisaties wereldwijd. Volgens de Amerikaanse regering faciliteerde A/I daarmee ‘antifa’, een afkorting voor ‘antifascisten’. De regering-Trump ziet antifa als een terroristische organisatie. A/I werd daarom eind augustus zelf ook als terroristisch bestempeld. Dat was een unicum. Internetdienstverleners worden in de regel niet verantwoordelijk gehouden voor de inhoud van wat hun gebruikers online zetten.

Als gevolg van de sanctie verloor de organisatie toegang tot zijn bankrekening en domeinnaam. Ruim een week na publicatie van de sanctie besloten de vrijwilligers die de internetdienstverlener runden om hun werk te staken en A/I te ontmantelen.

Amerikaans rechtshulpverzoek

Zo wilden ze voorkomen dat ze mensen of organisaties in de problemen zouden brengen omdat die banden met hen hadden, bijvoorbeeld doordat ze donateur waren of gebruik maakten van de webhosting of e-mail van A/I.

De inbeslagname van de server in Amsterdam duidt erop dat die angst niet ongegrond is. De politie in Amsterdam liet de server ophalen op basis van een Amerikaans rechtshulpverzoek. „Dat voer je dan gewoon uit”, zegt een woordvoerder telefonisch. Digitale experts van de politie maken er nu een ‘image’ van, een digitale kopie. „Die gaat linea recta naar Amerika.” Daarna krijgen de eigenaren de server terug.

A/I had servers op verschillende locaties in Europa staan. De afgelopen weken zijn die gesloten en zijn de schijven gewist, vertelt een betrokkene, die om veiligheidsredenen alleen anoniem praat. Het opheffen en ontmantelen van de juridische entiteit – A/I is een soort stichting – vergt wat tijd, licht hij toe. Een kleine groep van de voormalige vrijwilligers houdt zich met de afhandeling van de opheffing bezig. Er is onderling zo min mogelijk contact.
